title: Testing Strategies
description: Testing strategies: unit, integration and end-to-end tests, TDD, test doubles and coverage that means something.
objectives: Write tests that fail for the right reason
Choose the right test level for each behaviour
Keep a suite fast enough that people actually run it

practice.title: SCENARIO 1: The unit test that passes alone and fails in the suite
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
a module-level mutable object in a *production* file (let cache = new Map() at module scope) that another test populated;
a test that mutates a shared fixture object imported from a factory module;
vi.mock of a module in one file leaking into another because the module registry is shared when isolate: false;
a real Date mutation: a test calls vi.setSystemTime(...) and a sibling reads Date.now();
a module-level process.env write with no vi.unstubAllEnvs().
Guardrail
sequence.shuffle in CI for the unit tier, with a fixed seed, so order dependence surfaces on the pipeline rather than on a colleague's machine.
A lint rule banning module-level let/const Map/Set in src/domain/.
test/setup-global.ts calling vi.resetModules(), vi.restoreAllMocks(), vi.unstubAllEnvs() in beforeEach (see Problem 1).
A test that asserts purity directly:
symptoms: pricing.spec.ts passes in isolation (npx vitest run src/domain/pricing.spec.ts) and about 1 in 8 times in the full suite, with a failure like expected 2500 to be 3000 on a discount calculation.
rootCause: src/domain/pricing.ts had a module-level memo:

practice.title: SCENARIO 2: The async test that hangs until the timeout, with no error
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
A promise chain that can never advance, because fake timers faked the microtask pump. Symptom: the test only hangs when vi.useFakeTimers() is active.
A waitFor that is waiting for something the app never does (a spinner that never resolves because the query is in error state, not loading).
An event listener the app registers but the test never triggers, so a state machine never leaves its first state.
Proof
Guardrail
Never call vi.useFakeTimers() in beforeAll. Scope it to the individual tests that need it, and restore in afterEach.
Narrow the faked API surface in config: toFake: ['setTimeout', 'clearTimeout', 'setInterval', 'clearInterval', 'Date']. Do not fake queueMicrotask, nextTick, or performance.
The timer-leak guard in test/setup-timers.ts (Problem 1) turns "hung with no error" into "5 timers still pending", which is actionable.
A testTimeout of 5s with a comment that it is a bug indicator, so a hang is a red build and not a mystery.
symptoms: checkout.test.tsx fails after 5 seconds with Test timed out in 5000ms. and an empty stack. No assertion error, no unhandled rejection.
rootCause: The test file's beforeAll called vi.useFakeTimers() globally "because the component has a spinner", and the component's submit path awaited a debounced setTimeout inside a useEffect. With setTimeout faked and never advanced, the promise never resolved. The spinner was also driven by a real timer.

practice.title: SCENARIO 3: The integration test that fails only on CI, and only sometimes
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
docker logs on the Postgres container during the failure: look for too many clients already, or nothing at all (meaning the connection never arrived, i.e. the pool was exhausted client-side).
Prisma logs at warn/info: the pool's connection_limit versus pool_timeout.
The failures correlate with worker count: raising maxWorkers raises the failure rate proportionally.
The failures cluster at the *start* of the run, when every worker is opening its pool at once.
Guardrail
Set the pool size explicitly. Never rely on a cpu-derived default in CI.
maxWorkers for integration must be a conscious number tied to the pool, not a CPU count.
Assert in the harness that no connection is left checked out after each test:
Add a query timeout so a hung query fails rather than blocking the pool: SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '10s' inside each test transaction.
symptoms: orders.api.test.ts fails on CI roughly 6% of runs with P2028: Transaction API error: Transaction already closed or P1001: Can't reach database server. Locally it is 100% green.
rootCause: Two causes stacked:

maxWorkers: 8 in the integration config against a Postgres container with max_connections = 100, but Prisma's *default* pool per worker is num_cpus * 2 + 1. On a 4-core runner that is 9 connections per worker, so 8 workers x 9 = 72, plus the setup connection, plus health checks, and a single test that leaks a transaction pushes it over. Worse, the VITEST_WORKER_ID-based database cloning meant 8 separate databases, each needing its own pool, on a container sized for the default 100.
A test that opened a transaction and never released it (an early return inside withRolledBackDb before the sentinel throw), so a connection stayed checked out for the rest of the worker.

practice.title: SCENARIO 4: The component test that fails on getByRole with "found multiple elements"
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis

Duplicate DOM. The redesign renders both a desktop and a mobile header, and CSS hides one. In jsdom, display: none is not applied by the external stylesheet at all, so both are "visible" to Testing Library. This is the key insight people miss: jsdom does not apply your CSS, so a visually-hidden element is queryable.
The tests are asserting on the wrong thing. A button labelled "Save" appears in the profile dialog, the billing form, and the notification drawer. The test means one specific button.
Guardrail
In the shared renderWithProviders, accept a viewport option and set the corresponding class, so viewport-dependent tests are explicit.
Prefer getByRole(..., { name }) with a *specific* name, or scope with within(region), over a global query.
Add a component test that asserts the count of landmarks and of each primary action, so a duplicate header is caught by a test whose purpose is structural:
In E2E, use getByRole there too, where CSS *is* applied -- so a Playwright test that passes and a jsdom test that fails is a signal about the duplication, not about the framework.
symptoms: After a redesign that added a mobile layout alongside the desktop one, 22 component tests fail with:
rootCause: The component duplicated markup for responsive layout, and the tests used a broad role+name query that is not unique in the product.
fix: Fix the component, not the tests -- but fix the tests too, because the duplication is a design problem and the broad query is a test problem.

practice.title: SCENARIO 5: The snapshot test that fails every time because of a timestamp
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
Remove the nondeterminism at the source, which is the only real fix:
Add a serializer as defence in depth, so any *remaining* volatile value does not require a human:
Guardrail
A lint rule or a review convention: no new Date(), Date.now(), Math.random(), or crypto.randomUUID() in code reachable from a snapshot test without an injected port.
In CI, --update=false, so a nondeterministic snapshot cannot regenerate itself into green.
A nightly job that re-runs the whole suite twice with different seeds; any snapshot that differs between the two runs fails, which catches nondeterminism the main run got lucky on.
Fail the build on obsolete snapshots, so .snap files do not accumulate entries nothing references:
symptoms: A newly added snapshot test fails on the second run in the same day with a diff containing only "createdAt": "2026-03-01T14:23:11.482Z" instead of "2026-03-01T14:23:09.117Z". It passed when committed.
rootCause: The production mapper read the real clock, so the test was inherently nondeterministic. The first run passed because the baseline was *generated* from that run (updateSnapshot: 'new'), which is exactly how nondeterministic snapshots enter a repository.

practice.title: SCENARIO 6: The E2E test that fails on the click with "element is not stable"
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
Guardrail
trace: 'retain-on-failure' in the Playwright config. This diagnosis took 20 minutes with a trace and would have taken a day without one.
An app-level "settled" signal (data-settled="true") on every view that depends on fetched data, so tests can wait for a state rather than for a duration.
expect on a *state* immediately before every action that can be preceded by a refetch. This is the single highest-leverage practice in E2E.
A component test asserting pointer-events on overlays, which is impossible to test in E2E but trivial in jsdom.
symptoms: checkout.spec.ts fails ~20% of the time with:
rootCause: The Place order button is inside a component that re-renders when the cart query refetches. Playwright resolves the element, then the node is replaced, then it tries to click a detached handle. The trace's DOM snapshots show the same button in two different container elements between the actionability check and the click. The tell in the trace is a network request (a React Query refetch) firing immediately before the failure.

A cookie banner, a toast, or a "prices updated" modal renders above the button. Playwright's hit test finds the overlay, not the button. The trace shows a banner or dialog element with a higher stacking order at the same coordinates.

practice.title: SCENARIO 7: The transaction-per-test suite that leaves data behind
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
Production code opened its own client. A module-level new PrismaClient() somewhere in the call path writes outside the test's transaction, so the test's rollback does not undo it.
Raw SQL on a separate connection. A pg Pool created at module scope for a reporting query, a full-text search index maintenance, or a pg_notify.

A non-transactional table. Postgres sequences and some extensions (pg_trgm indexes are transactional, but a MATERIALIZED VIEW and some queue tables are not). If a fixture writes to one, the rollback leaves it.
A worker thread or a background job started by the application under test, holding its own pool.
$executeRawUnsafe('TRUNCATE') somewhere committing outside the test transaction.
Guardrail
The explicit PID assertion above, once, in a dedicated test: *"every database write in a request happens on the request's connection"*. That is a load-bearing invariant and it deserves its own test.
A dependency-boundary lint rule: src/infrastructure/ may not new a Pool or PrismaClient at module scope. It must be constructed in the composition root and injected.
The idle-in-transaction leak assertion in afterEach (Scenario 3), which catches the *other* direction.
A CI hygiene job: run the integration suite twice in a row on the same database. A suite that only passes on a fresh database is broken, and this is the cheapest possible detector.
symptoms: The integration suite is green on a clean database and fails on the second run with a unique-constraint violation on User_email_key, at the fixture creation step.
rootCause: A SearchIndexer class created its own pg.Pool at module scope to write to a search_documents table outside the application transaction, on the assumption that indexing must not be rolled back. The write was outside the test transaction and therefore survived the rollback.

practice.title: SCENARIO 8: The MSW test that passes against a handler the real API never serves
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
Capture real responses from the provider's sandbox (three: success, decline, 3DS challenge) and store them as fixtures.
Type the fake's return type against the provider's own TypeScript definitions, if they exist.
Generate the MSW handlers from the provider's OpenAPI schema, so a required field the handler omits is a type error.
Record real fixtures and make the fake return them verbatim.
Type the client's mapping as a total function over the observed statuses, so a new status is a compile error rather than a silent success:
A nightly sandbox smoke test, which is what keeps the fixtures honest:
Guardrail
Handlers live in one module imported by tests, Storybook, and dev, and are derived from recorded fixtures wherever the provider can be reached.
onUnhandledRequest: 'error', so a handler with a wrong URL fails loudly.
A test that asserts the client's behaviour for every documented provider outcome, including the unknown-shape case, so a new status cannot fall through to success.

A reviewed registry of third-party contracts, each with: recorded fixtures, a schema, a nightly smoke test, and an owner. A third party with no entry in the registry is a third party you do not understand.
symptoms: A checkout test passes with MSW stubbing POST /api/payments/charge returning 200 { id: 'ch_1' }. In production, roughly 30% of charges are declined and the client treats every non-200 as success, so declined payments are recorded as paid. No test fails.
rootCause: The handler was written from memory of what "a payment API" returns, not from the provider's actual contract. The client code had a branch that treated any 2xx as success, and no test ever produced a non-2xx from the fake.

practice.title: SCENARIO 9: The test suite that got 5x slower after a framework upgrade
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
All tests equally slower by a constant factor: something per-test. A new per-test setup cost (a schema validation, a config reload, a new client construction) or a lost parallelism.
A few tests disproportionately slower: a specific pattern is now expensive (N+1 awaits, a serialised query, a re-render per keystroke).
CPU-bound (high process CPU, low I/O wait): the runner or a transform.
Wall-time-bound with idle CPU: a fixed sleep or a retry backoff.
Guardrail
A per-file duration report in CI, posted to the job summary, so a 3x regression is visible in the diff rather than felt.
A duration budget with an alert:
A baseline for the slow-test list, with a check that new entries require an explicit // @slow comment and a justification.
A dependency upgrade policy: upgrade on a branch, run the suite, and diff the per-file durations. A 20% regression requires a written explanation before merge.
symptoms: After upgrading a query library, the component suite went from 50 seconds to 4 minutes, and 14 tests now time out. No test logic changed.
rootCause: Two causes from the upgrade:
The library's new version validates the whole query key on every invalidateQueries call, and three tests invalidate a large keyset in a loop. That is the few-slow-tests pattern.
The new version logs a deprecation warning per instantiation, and the test setup's onConsoleLog gate was serialising console writes through a reporter. That is the all-tests pattern.

practice.title: SCENARIO 10: The E2E test that only fails in Firefox
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
A different default box model or sizing. Firefox's default box-sizing differs for some elements, or a width: 100% plus padding overflows differently, so the button is positioned differently.
A different default line-height/font-size, which changes text wrapping and therefore element height, which moves what overlaps.
A scroll container difference. Firefox scrolls a nested container where Chromium scrolls the page, so the sticky header covers the focused element (WCAG 2.4.11).
A <form> submit difference, or a <button> outside a form behaving differently.
A real engine difference: Intl output, a CSS feature Firefox does not support, form validation UI, or date parsing.
Guardrail
Run every E2E journey in all three engines on main, not just on PRs. A Firefox-only bug found after release is a Firefox-only bug found too late.
A visual-regression baseline per platform, generated in a pinned container. Cross-engine layout drift is a visual signal, and it is much cheaper to see than to debug.
Never use force: true in a click. It is the E2E equivalent of a type cast: it silences a real overlap or hit-test problem.
A project-wide rule: after every user action, either assert a state or assert a visibility precondition. click() with nothing after it is where these bugs hide.
symptoms: A checkout test passes in Chromium, fails 100% of the time in Firefox with locator.click: element intercepts pointer events on the submit button. WebKit passes.
rootCause: A sticky header with z-index: 10 and a position: sticky inside a page where the payment form's submit button sat at the very top of the viewport after scrolling. Chromium scrolled the page; Firefox scrolled an inner <main> element with its own overflow, so the sticky header ended up overlaying the button. The overlay was the header, not a toast.

practice.title: SCENARIO 11: The test that is green but the feature is broken
items: Reproduction
Diagnosis
Guardrail
Mutation testing in CI on changed files. A surviving mutant in a changed file is a code review comment with evidence attached. This is the instrument that catches "green but wrong".
expect(result).toEqual({...}) on small value objects rather than field-by-field assertions, so a *new* field forces a decision.
A review question that is asked every time: *"what test covers the combination of these two branches?"* If nobody can answer, the test does not exist.

Property-based tests for the general version of the same problem: for a large input space, assert invariants (monotonicity in subtotalCents, discount <= maxDiscountPercent, total + discount === subtotal, coupons never stack) rather than enumerating cases.
symptoms: pricing.test.ts is 100% covered, all green, and a promotion gives the wrong discount in production for orders above GBP 500. No test ever exercised a case where a tier is expired *and* a coupon is applied.
rootCause: Two specific defects in the suite:
Each test set up one condition. it('applies no expired tier'), it('applies a coupon') -- but never it('does not apply a coupon to an expired tier'). The combination is where the bug was.

The assertions were weak. expect(result.discountCents).toBeGreaterThan(0) instead of expect(result).toEqual({ subtotalCents: 60000, discountCents: 12000, appliedCoupon: null, reason: 'tier_expired' }).

practice.title: SCENARIO 12: The pipeline that takes 45 minutes and developers have learned to batch
items: Reproduction and diagnosis
The result
Guardrail
A pipeline duration budget, posted to the job summary every run, with an alert if the p50 exceeds it. The budget is what stops the slow creep back.
Per-job duration history stored and charted, so a regression is a visual event, not a feeling.
A quarterly review of the *shape* of the suite: tests per tier, and the ratio of E2E to total. If E2E crosses 15% of the test count, that is a finding.

A rule that a PR which is "big because CI is slow" is a signal to split the PR, not to raise the timeout. Every timeout raised to make CI pass is a hidden decision about what your tests actually verify.
symptoms: CI takes 38-52 minutes per PR. Developers open one PR per day containing four features, review is perfunctory, and about 4% of PRs are reverted after merge. Nobody has raised this as a problem because "CI is slow" is normalised.
rootCause: Four compounding problems:
retries: 2 in Playwright plus a 2.5% flake rate, so the effective E2E time was 9 min x 1.5 on average, and one failing shard meant 12 minutes before a human saw anything.
The preview environment was deployed per PR push, including pushes that only changed a README.
practice.reference:
```bash
# 1. Per-job durations for the last 50 runs.
gh run list --limit 50 --json databaseId,conclusion,createdAt,jobs \
  --jq '.[] | {id: .databaseId, at: .createdAt, jobs: [.jobs[] | {name, duration: (.startedAt)}]}' \
  > ci-history.json

# 2. Aggregate.
node -e "
const runs = require('./ci-history.json')
const totals = new Map()
for (const r of runs) for (const j of r.jobs || []) {
  totals.set(j.name, (totals.get(j.name) || 0) + (new Date(j.duration) - new Date(j.startedAt)) / 60000)
}
;[...totals.entries()].sort((a,b)=>b[1]-a[1]).forEach(([n,m])=>console.log(m.toFixed(1).padStart(8), 'min avg  ', n))
console.log('\nruns:', runs.length, ' failures:', runs.filter(r=>r.conclusion!=='success').length)
"
```

```yaml
# 1. Cache the browsers. Saves 7 minutes per job.
- name: Cache Playwright browsers
  id: pw-cache
  uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.cache/ms-playwright
    key: pw-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}-${{ hashFiles('playwright.config.ts') }}
    restore-keys: pw-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}-
- run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
  if: steps.pw-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
```

```yaml
# 2. Reuse the preview environment per branch; redeploy only when the build or the
#    migrations change. A docs-only push now skips E2E entirely.
- name: Detect whether anything that affects the app changed
  id: scope
  run: |
    if git diff --quiet origin/main...HEAD -- src/ prisma/ package.json; then
      echo "changed=app"   >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    elif git diff --quiet origin/main...HEAD; then
      echo "changed=none"  >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    else
      echo "changed=docs"  >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    fi
- run: npx acme/deploy-preview --if-changed ${{ steps.scope.outputs.changed }}
```

```ts
// 3. Move 108 tests down a tier. The CRUD and validation-message checks become component
//    tests; 4 E2E journeys remain.
test.describe('orders', () => {
  test('@smoke a customer places an order and sees it in their history', ...)      // 3 min
  test('a declined card does not create an order and preserves the input', ...)     // 40s
  test('a 3DS challenge completes the payment', ...)                               // 50s

```

```yaml
# 4. E2E policy: Chromium on every user-facing PR; all three engines on main only.
e2e:
  needs: [build, scope]
  if: >-
    steps.scope.outputs.changed == 'app' &&
    (github.event_name == 'push' || contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'e2e'))
  strategy:
    fail-fast: false
    matrix: { shard: [1, 2] }          # 4 -> 2 shards: the suite is now 60 tests, not 180
  steps:
    - run: pnpm exec playwright test --project=chromium --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/2
```

# 5. Flake: fix, do not retry. Track it.
- uses: playwrightwright/test@...   # retries: 1 in CI, and a flake budget that fails the build
- run: node scripts/flake-budget.mjs test-results/e2e-results.json

questions.text: 🟢 Beginner · Must-know — What is a unit test, and how is it different from an integration test?
questions.answer: A unit test exercises one cohesive piece of logic through its public surface, with every collaborator substituted so that it is deterministic, isolated and fast: no network, no real clock, no real database, no Math.random. An integration test crosses at least one *real* boundary -- a real database, a real HTTP server, a real queue -- and verifies that two or more components interoperate correctly. The test I would run to settle any argument is: *can I run this with zero network, zero disk and zero database?* If yes, it is a unit test. The second test is: *would this still pass if I rewrote the implementation with different internals but identical observable behaviour?* If yes, it is testing behaviour, which is what I want; if no, it is coupled to implementation and will be a tax on every refactor. I would add the nuance that "unit" is genuinely ambiguous -- function, class, module, or behaviour are four defensible definitions -- and that the productive framing is the *behavioural* one: a unit is one observable rule the system promises, regardless of how many functions implement it.

questions.text: 🟢 Beginner · Must-know — Explain the AAA pattern and when you would stop using it.
questions.answer: AAA is Arrange, Act, Assert: build the preconditions, do exactly one thing, then assert one logical outcome. Its value is navigability -- a stranger can find each phase in a glance -- and blame: a failing test names the phase it died in. I would stop using it as a *comment convention* for tests that are two lines long. expect(isValid(x)).toBe(true) does not need three comment blocks. And I would never let an arrange helper contain the Act, because then the failure is attributed to the wrong place and the reader is misled. The real limit is one Act per test. Two acts mean two behaviours, and if the second depends on the first's state you cannot assert the first in isolation. When I see a test called "checkout works" with fourteen assertions, I treat it as four tests that have not been separated yet.

questions.text: 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know — What is a test double, and how do mock, stub, spy and fake differ?
questions.answer: A test double is anything standing in for a real dependency. A dummy satisfies a signature and does nothing. A stub returns canned data so the code under test can run; you do not care how it was called. A spy delegates to the real implementation and records the calls. A mock returns canned data *and* you assert on how it was called. A fake is a working but deliberately simplified implementation with real semantics -- an in-memory repository, a clock you can advance, a payment gateway that declines a specific card. The distinction that matters for quality is state verification versus behaviour verification. Prefer asserting on the *output* the code produced; use interaction assertions only when the interaction is genuinely the contract, like "publishes exactly one order.paid event". A mock-heavy suite is one where the mocks' return values have become the specification, and that specification is wrong the moment the interface changes. My default is fakes, because they support state verification and survive refactors. I reach for mocks when I need to assert on an outward-facing event.

questions.text: 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know — What is property-based testing, and when is it better than example tests?
questions.answer: Property-based testing inverts the question. Instead of "does this function return the right thing for this input", you state invariants that must hold for *every* input, provide generators for the input domain, and let the framework shrink any counterexample to a minimal failing case. With fast-check the workflow is generate, assert, and on failure report a minimal input plus a reproducible seed. I use it when the input space is large and the rule is a property rather than a case: parsers and serialisers (round-trip), allocators and splitters (conservation plus fairness -- a payment split must sum to the total with no share differing by more than one cent), reducers (associativity and identity), anything with money or dates or codecs. I write the example tests alongside it, because stakeholders care about specific cases ("GBP 100 gets 10% off") and a property is documentation only its author fully understands. The cost is authoring: generators need thought about cross-field invariants, and I budget two to five times a single example test.

questions.text: 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know — What does code coverage actually measure, and what does it miss?
questions.answer: Coverage measures which executable constructs -- lines, branches, functions, statements -- your suite *executed*. It is a meta-metric about the test suite, not a measure of quality or correctness. What it misses is the important part. It cannot see whether your test had any assertions, so expect(f(1)).toBeDefined() gives 100% coverage and zero signal. It cannot see whether your expectations are *correct*, which is the worst possible state to be in. It says nothing about interleavings and races, about performance, or about whether the deployed configuration is right. A function at 100% coverage may have all its if branches untested while every line ran. So I use coverage for three things only: detecting dead code, finding untested error paths, and gating *new* uncovered lines in a PR with diff coverage. I do not use it as a target for engineers, because that reliably produces assertion-free code, and I pair it with mutation testing as the real quality signal.

questions.text: 🟡 Intermediate · Must-know — When is a snapshot test the right choice, and how do you stop it rotting?
questions.answer: A snapshot test is right for large, deterministic, reviewable outputs where writing explicit assertions would be enormous and unmaintainable: generated OpenAPI documents and GraphQL schemas, serialised state, state-machine traces, translation key sets, and rendered pixels. The value is that a diff is a *change detector*: it tells you that everything you did not intend did not change. The failure mode is noise, and noise is fatal. A snapshot nobody reads protects nothing. So: normalise every volatile field with a serializer -- dates, uuids, ids, hashes, Errors, and object key order; keep snapshots small and inline so the diff appears in the same review as the code; pair every snapshot with three to five explicit assertions on the invariants that actually matter; never auto-update in CI; and fail the build on obsolete entries so .snap files do not accumulate junk. The rule I hold to: if a snapshot is too large to read in a PR diff, it should be replaced with explicit assertions.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What is TDD, and where does it *not* pay off?
questions.answer: TDD is a discipline: write a failing test first, make it pass in the simplest way possible, then refactor with the test as a safety net, in small steps. The green step is deliberately throwaway -- I hardcode the return value first to prove my test can actually pass, which isolates a failure of the test from a failure of the implementation. That step feels like cheating and is the most misunderstood part. It pays off where the domain has rules and edge cases, where the implementation will be rewritten, where a bug is expensive, and where you have continuous integration so the suite is trustworthy. It does not pay off when you are exploring an unknown design, when the unit is framework wiring whose value is in the integration, when UI layout is the deliverable, on a hard deadline with fixed scope, or in a team large enough that coordination dominates. One nuance I would add: TDD's cost is paid in the first twenty percent of the work and recovered in the rest -- the evidence is strongest on debug time and API design quality rather than defect count. And bad tests make TDD actively harmful, because you end up with a green suite protecting the wrong behaviour, having *also* paid the cost of writing the test first.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What are the four ways an async test lies about time?
questions.answer: One: the test finishes before the async work does -- a missing await, or an await on the wrong promise, so you assert on an unresolved value. The symptom is a test that passes even when the code is broken, and the fix is awaiting the returned promise plus expect.assertions(n) to prove you waited. Two: real time is slower than the test's patience. A real setTimeout(50) in a test is a 1% flake rate on a loaded CI machine. The fix is to eliminate real time -- either inject a Clock into your own code, which I strongly prefer, or use fake timers for code you do not own. Three: the classic one -- you advance the clock synchronously. vi.advanceTimersByTime(1000) fires the timer callbacks but any await inside them is queued as a microtask that has not run, so your assertion sees the state from *before* the callback completed. The fix is await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1000), which drains the microtask queue between callbacks. Four: leaked timers. The code schedules something and never clears it, so the test ends with a pending timer; Jest prints "worker failed to exit gracefully" and the next test is polluted. The fix is that production code must clear on teardown, and the test asserts vi.getTimerCount() === 0.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — How do you decide where the test seams go?
questions.answer: Along the lines of *reasoning and effect*, not along lines of files. I inject a port when the thing is an effect -- I/O, the clock, randomness, the network, a message bus -- and when substituting it buys me determinism or a test of its own. I do not inject for its own sake; an interface with one implementation and one test is ceremony. The specific seams I nearly always want are Clock and Random, because they are the two collaborators that most often lie, and injecting them turns time-based rules -- session expiry, retry backoff, scheduled jobs, token TTL -- into instant, exact, order-deterministic tests with no fake timers at all. Beyond that: a PaymentGateway, a Mailer, a repository, and an id generator. A useful smell test: if I find myself mocking my own domain module, the seam is in the wrong place and the logic should be extracted to a pure function instead.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — When would you use transaction-per-test isolation, and what can you not test with it?
questions.answer: Transaction-per-test is the highest-leverage decision in a Postgres-backed integration suite. You open a transaction before the test, bind your code to a client bound to that transaction, and roll back afterwards instead of deleting rows. It is ten to a hundred times faster than truncate-and-reseed, it preserves *real* transactional semantics during the test, and it makes tests order-independent and parallel-safe against one shared database for free. What you cannot test with it: anything on a second connection or process. Background workers, because their writes are outside your transaction. Self-HTTP calls. Two-concurrent-writer scenarios, where neither actor sees the other's uncommitted data. Advisory locks and LISTEN/NOTIFY, which are session-scoped. SERIALIZABLE conflicts. And commit-visibility semantics. There is one more gap worth naming: it hides whether your code commits correctly. If a repository's multi-statement write is not atomic, a transactional suite will not catch it, because the test's own rollback masks the partial write. You need one non-transactional test per repository that forces the second statement to fail and asserts the first did not land.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — Why is MSW better than mocking your own API client?
questions.answer: Because MSW intercepts at the network boundary, so *your* code runs for real. Mocking PaymentGateway.charge means the URL, the headers, the auth, the payload serialisation, the timeout handling, the retry logic and the error mapping are all untested -- you have replaced exactly the code most likely to be wrong with a return value you chose. MSW stubs the third party's HTTP API, so your adapter is under test. The two properties I hold onto: the handler's response shape must be a *recorded* real response, not something I invented from memory, and onUnhandledRequest: 'error' must be set, so a handler with a wrong URL fails immediately instead of silently producing a 404 from the wrong place. The honest limitation is that MSW proves you speak the protocol you *think* the provider speaks. I close that gap with contract tests derived from the published spec, and a nightly suite against the provider's real sandbox that re-checks the recorded shapes.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What is consumer-driven contract testing, and when is it not worth it?
questions.answer: The consumer's tests run against a mock provider generated from a pact, the pact is published to a broker, and the provider's CI replays every consumer pact against its real API before deploying. The genuinely novel part is that the consumer can build and test in parallel with no shared environment, and the provider learns *before* deploy which specific interaction is about to break. The matcher choice is the real design decision, and I decide it by asking what the consumer's code does with the field. A field it branches on -- status -- gets equality or a regex enum, so a new enum value shows up as a contract change. A free-text display name gets type or a length regex, because pinning a value the consumer never reads makes the contract brittle for no benefit. A collection gets eachLike. A possibly-absent field gets nullOrType. It is not worth it with one monolithic codebase, where an integration test is cheaper and stronger; when the "services" are really modules in one repo; or when the API churns so much you cannot afford the operational cost of a pact platform.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — How do you test authorisation properly?
questions.answer: I test the negative path first, because almost every authorisation breach is a missing return, an || where && was meant, a query that filters by id but not by userId, or a scope check that runs after the data is returned. A positive-path test passes on code with no authorisation at all. Four patterns, four tests. Route guards: derive the route list from the router itself and assert every route returns 401 without a token, so a new route added without a guard fails the build. Role and scope: generate a role-by-action matrix from the permission table and assert each cell, so the matrix cannot drift. Object-level ownership: create two users' objects and assert user A gets a 404 -- not a 403 -- for user B's, because 403 confirms the record exists. Tenant isolation: identical object ids in two tenants, and assert cross-tenant reads fail; that is the only way to catch a missing filter. I never mock the auth middleware in a test I am using to prove authorisation works. I sign a real token with the test secret, and I forbid x-test-user bypass headers, because that is a permanent backdoor.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What is a flaky test, and what is your process for eliminating them?
questions.answer: A flaky test is one that passes and fails for the same code. Flake is not a nuisance; it is the largest destroyer of suite value. At 5% flake the effective gate is near zero, because developers learn to re-run and reviewers stop reading. My process is ordered. First, classify by reproduction: run with --repeat.each 200 for order dependence, vary workers for parallelism, run the suite twice for data dependence, and run under load for timing. Then, classify the cause into eleven buckets -- missing await, shared state, real timers, unseeded randomness, resource exhaustion, environment drift, external dependencies, leftover data, over-broad selectors, concurrency, and framework bugs. Then I fix by class, and add the guard that prevents recurrence: expect.assertions(n) for missing awaits, beforeEach state for shared state, a FakeClock for timers, a seed for randomness, and afterEach guards for timers and unhandled rejections. Anything unresolved gets quarantined with test.skip, a linked ticket, a named owner and a due date, and CI fails if the quarantine list grows. I never delete a flaky test silently, and I never set retries above one. A high-retry suite is decoration: the failure mode is that a real regression passes on the third attempt and nobody investigates.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — Why is Vitest faster than Jest, and what are the semantic differences in migrating?
questions.answer: Four independent reasons. Vitest reuses Vite's module graph and esbuild-based transform instead of Babel or ts-jest compiling every file to CJS per worker, which is the single biggest cost in Jest. It keeps native ESM rather than paying interop on every mock boundary. It pools in threads with a warm server, so a watch-mode re-run only re-transforms what changed. And it offers a real browser environment, which removes the jsdom fidelity gap. The practical number is the dev loop, not the suite: eight seconds down to 0.4 seconds for an edit-to-result cycle. That changes engineering behaviour -- people run tests after every edit instead of once before pushing. Three semantic differences bite on migration. Fake timer defaults differ: Vitest fakes more APIs by default, so I narrow with toFake. alias applies to all imports including in dependencies, so a node_modules mock may also need server.deps.inline. And ESM mocks are per module graph, not per require call, so "mock only for this test" needs vi.resetModules() plus vi.doMock plus a dynamic import. I would stage the migration with a global alias in setup, run both runners side by side for a week comparing result sets, and never do it in the same PR as a feature change.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — How do you test code that depends on time, randomness and concurrency?
questions.answer: I inject ports. Clock for time, Random for randomness with a seedable implementation, and a Scheduler for timers. That turns token expiry, retry backoff and scheduled jobs into instant, exact, order-deterministic tests with no fake timers, and it is the only approach that scales to *ordering* tests. For concurrency specifically, I do not assert on one interleaving. I model the race as a state machine and assert the invariant that holds under all interleavings -- for example, that a balance never goes negative regardless of the order two debits arrive in. Where the race is genuinely about ordering, I inject a Yield or deferred helper so I can control the interleaving deterministically rather than hoping. The design consequence is that every module needs the port threaded through. That is a cost paid once and refunded forever, and it is the right investment in any system with a time rule -- sessions, retries, billing, caches, jobs.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What belongs in an E2E test, and what does not?
questions.answer: E2E verifies the parts no other tier can see: the actual bundle that ships, the service worker, the CSP and CORS configuration, the reverse proxy and TLS, real cookie flags, third-party scripts, browser storage, the auth redirect, and the fact that the pieces are wired together at all. It is a *sample* of journeys, not exhaustive coverage. What it must not do is verify business rules. Discount arithmetic belongs in property-based unit tests where it runs five thousand times in forty milliseconds; in E2E you can check one example. It must not cover layout exhaustively -- that is component tests plus visual regression. And it must not be the only feedback loop: a developer waiting six minutes to learn their typo broke the build has been taught to batch work, and batching is how defects enter. I hold a budget: ten to thirty E2E tests per major journey, under ten minutes wall clock, with a flake rate under half a percent. A healthy E2E suite is small, and *shrinking* it is a sign of a maturing test strategy.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — Explain Playwright's locator model and auto-waiting.
questions.answer: A locator is a lazy, auto-retrying query. Nothing happens until you act or assert, and each action polls the locator until the element is actionable -- visible, stable, not animating, enabled, and receiving pointer events -- or the timeout expires. Assertions poll the same way, which is why expect(locator).toBeVisible() is a real wait and not a sleep. The priority order is by accessibility: role plus accessible name first, then label, then placeholder, then text, and getByTestId only as a last resort with an explanatory comment. The reason is that role-and-name queries are the user's contract, and a component you cannot query by role is usually a component a screen-reader user cannot operate. So the suite doubles as an accessibility smoke test. The two things that defeat auto-waiting: waiting for a state the app never expresses in the DOM -- a JavaScript condition unrelated to the render -- and waitForTimeout, which is always a defect. And the isolation primitive is the BrowserContext: an incognito-like profile with its own cookies, storage, permissions and locale, created in about fifty milliseconds versus a second for a new browser. That is what makes per-test isolation affordable, and it is why fullyParallel is feasible.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What is sharding, and what is the mistake people make with it?
questions.answer: Sharding splits the test set into N groups that run in parallel, so wall clock falls roughly as 1/N. The mistake is assuming it balances. Playwright and Vitest both shard by *file count*, not by duration, so one spec file that takes six minutes makes one shard five times longer than the others and the whole exercise buys nothing. The fix is to measure and rebalance: run once with a JSON reporter, group per-test durations by file, and bin-pack the files into N groups by total duration. Then split the slow spec into smaller files so future sharding behaves. I also always set fail-fast: false on a test matrix, because cancelling the sibling shards destroys exactly the traces you need. And I only shard when there is enough duration to justify the coordination. A ninety-second suite sharded four ways is pure overhead.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — When do you use a Page Object, and when does it hide the test?
questions.answer: The original intent was to keep selectors in one place. The more useful modern framing is *capability objects* over *page objects*: a capability models an intentional set of actions that may cross screens -- checkout.addToBasket('Widget').openBasket().payWithCard(card).confirm() -- so the test body reads as the user journey and every selector lives in exactly one file. Screen-scoped page objects multiply: a six-screen flow means six objects, and the test reads like a script again. It hides the test when the object returns data and the test asserts everything -- the object becomes a getter bag. When it contains business logic, which then drifts from the unit test that owns it. When it contains retries or try/catch, which makes a broken app look like a passing test. And when it is a one-line wrapper, which is pure indirection. My rule: extract when a flow is used by three or more tests, and keep a three-step straight-line test inline. Assertions about the *screen's* state belong with the screen's capability; assertions about persisted state belong in the test.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What is mutation testing, and why does it matter if you already have coverage?
questions.answer: Mutation testing measures whether your tests can actually *detect bugs*. The tool mutates an operator in your code -- >= to >, && to ||, return x to return null, a boundary to a boundary-plus-one -- and reruns the tests. If a mutant is killed, your tests detect that class of change. If it survives, you have a gap that coverage cannot see, because coverage only knows a line ran. That is precisely the point: coverage counts execution, mutation counts detection. A function at 100% coverage whose test asserts nothing has a mutation score near zero. Coverage is a cheap proxy; mutation score is the real quality signal, and it is what catches the "green but wrong" suite. Practically I scope it to files with fast tests, because mutating a file whose only coverage is integration tests produces a wall of meaningless escaped mutants. I set per-mutator thresholds that weight the informative mutants -- conditionals, boundaries, nullish coalescing -- above the noisy ones, like property reads and object literals. On PRs I run it on changed files only, nightly I run it exhaustively with a rising baseline, and I publish surviving mutants in the PR as a work list.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — How do you structure a CI testing pipeline?
questions.answer: Ordered by value per second. First, the fast gate: lint, typecheck, unit and property tests, and diff coverage -- target under three minutes, hard required, nobody waits for it. Second, integration with real services, which can run in parallel with the build because it does not depend on it. Third, build once and reuse the artefact everywhere downstream. Fourth, E2E smoke on a cached environment, then full E2E sharded against a preview environment built from the PR's artefact. Fifth, accessibility and performance, which for a front-end are first-class gates, not extras. Sixth, security scanning with a ratchet policy. Seventh, a nightly stage for everything expensive: all three browsers, full mutation, soak testing, DAST, provider smoke tests. Two decisions carry most of the value. The merge gate is one aggregator job that reads actual job results, because branch protection cannot express "these three of five jobs are required, and E2E only on main and on user-facing changes" -- so E2E and a11y are advisory on a PR unless the change is labelled user-facing, and always required on main. And fail-fast: false on every test matrix, because cancelling a sibling shard destroys the trace that would have told you what went wrong.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What is the test pyramid, what is the test trophy, and which do you use?
questions.answer: The pyramid is the empirical observation that fast isolated tests are cheap in every dimension while slow real-system tests are expensive, giving a shape of many units, fewer integrations, few E2E. The trophy is Kent Dodds' counter-proposal for front-ends: a thin base of static analysis and unit tests, a thick middle of component and integration tests, and very few E2E -- on the grounds that front-end risk lives in the wiring, not in the logic. For a back-end service with real domain rules and data access I use the pyramid. For a React application I use the trophy, because the failures that actually happen -- a provider is missing, a query key is wrong, a form's error state is unreachable, a route guard is absent -- are exactly what a component test with real providers and MSW catches in four hundred milliseconds. For a library I would invert it: most tests exercise the public API realistically, not internals. The honest framing is that both shapes are consequences of cost, not doctrines. The rule I apply to any behaviour is: put it in the cheapest tier that can genuinely detect its failure. The shape falls out of that.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What are the economics of a test suite, and how do you know which tests pay?
questions.answer: The cost of a tier over a year is engineering hours to write and maintain, plus CI minutes times rerun rate times triage minutes per failure, plus the value of the bugs it catches. And the dominant term is usually *triage*, not runtime. In a typical front-end project, an E2E failure costs forty-five minutes of a human's attention against three minutes for a component failure -- which is why the argument is always for fewer E2E tests, not more. A test earns its place when it maps to a stated behaviour, it fails when that behaviour breaks, it is deterministic and fast enough to run often, its maintenance cost is bounded, and no cheaper tier covers it. I verify the second condition with mutation testing rather than by assertion. The practical consequence is a budget: sixty to seventy percent of effort in the two cheap tiers, twenty to thirty in integration, and under ten percent in E2E. If E2E is more than about fifteen percent of your test count, you are using the most expensive instrument for work that cheaper ones do better.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — How do you test error and failure paths?
questions.answer: I keep a catalogue of every production incident I have had, and every entry becomes a test, because every incident is a test I did not write. The classes I need to be able to produce are: downstream 4xx and 5xx, downstream timeout, a real connection reset, a malformed response, a slow dependency, a database constraint violation or killed backend, resource exhaustion and rate limits, and partial success in a batch. Each has a distinct assertion set. For a 5xx I assert the retry count, the backoff, and that the error kind is *retryable*. For a 4xx I assert no retry and that it is classified as a permanent rejection. For a timeout I assert a bounded elapsed time and that no partial state was written. For a reset I assert it is a transport error, not a 500. For a malformed body I assert 502 with a generic message and no JSON.parse internals leaked. Two things I insist on. First, the negative space: for every failure, assert that the side effect did *not* happen. Second, observability: assert the log line exists with the request id, contains no PII and no secrets, and that the metric was incremented with a label that will not melt the metrics backend. And I use the real thing where possible: MSW for protocol-level failures, and a local socket server that destroys the connection for genuine transport failures, because route.abort cannot produce a real reset.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What accessibility testing is actually required, and what does automation miss?
questions.answer: Three layers, and only the first is automatable. Automated scanning -- axe-core in lint, component tests and E2E, plus Lighthouse and Pa11y -- catches the objective errors: missing labels, contrast, invalid ARIA, missing alt, heading order, duplicate ids. Manual expert testing -- keyboard only, a screen reader, zoom and reflow, forced colours, reduced motion, target size -- catches the rest. And user testing with disabled people catches whether the experience is actually usable. I run axe in three places deliberately: lint for authoring-time errors, component tests on key *states* (initial, error, empty, modal open), and E2E on the assembled critical pages. Initial-state-only scanning misses most bugs, because modals, menus and error states are where a11y problems live. Automation is necessary and not sufficient. It has a five to fifteen percent false-positive rate and a sixty to eighty percent false-negative rate. A clean axe report is not compliance, and it is certainly not accessibility. The legal frame matters too: the European Accessibility Act has applied since June 2025 to a broad range of consumer-facing digital products, and WCAG 2.2's new AA criteria -- focus not obscured, dragging movements, target size, accessible authentication -- catch things older tooling never flagged.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What security testing belongs in a pipeline, and what is its weakest link?
questions.answer: Four techniques, each covering what the others miss. SAST analyses source and finds injection patterns, insecure crypto and dangerous sinks. DAST attacks a running app and finds runtime and configuration issues -- security headers, cookie flags, CORS, real injection through a real path. SCA analyses the lockfile for known CVEs. Secret scanning finds committed credentials, and it must scan history, not just the current tree. The weakest link is policy, not tooling. A scanner that reports four hundred findings nobody fixes is worse than no scanner, because the first week of noise gets it muted forever. So the pattern is a baselined, ratcheting policy: triage once into a checked-in baseline with justifications, gate only on *new* high and critical findings, fail the build if the baseline contains entries that no longer match a finding, and track the count weekly. A rising count is a signal to act. The second weakest link is authorisation logic, which SAST fundamentally cannot see. It is pattern matching; it cannot know that findById should also filter by tenantId. That is covered by the generated role-by-action matrix and the object-level tests, and by a threat model -- and I would say so plainly rather than implying a green security pipeline means the app is secure.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — What does static analysis buy you, and what are the highest-value rules?
questions.answer: Three layers: linting, type checking, and program analysis for architectural constraints. The highest-value single setting in most JavaScript projects is TypeScript, because it verifies contracts across module boundaries that no test asserts. Within it, the flags that find the most real bugs are strictNullChecks and the rest of the strict family, noUncheckedIndexedAccess -- which makes arr[0].id a possible production TypeError -- and exactOptionalPropertyTypes, which stops a spread from smuggling undefined over a default. The single highest-value ESLint rule in an async codebase is @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises, because a bare saveUser(x) that a human reads as fine is how unhandled rejections happen. Program analysis is the layer most teams skip, and it is the one that prevents rot: I forbid domain modules from depending on the framework, forbid application depending on infrastructure, forbid test-support being imported by production code, and fail on import cycles. Those four rules mean the first big refactor is possible. On type-aware linting: it is three to ten times slower than the syntactic version, so I run fast rules in the editor and the full set in CI, and I expect to tune rules that produce false positives on generic-heavy code rather than muting them permanently.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — How do you make test data safe, and what is the GDPR position?
questions.answer: Test data is personal data if it identifies a natural person, so the lawful basis question is real, and "it is only in a test environment" is not an answer. Copying production data into a test database is a processing activity that usually also breaches the DPA, and it enlarges the blast radius of any breach for no real benefit. So the default is synthetic data, made *obviously* synthetic: reserved-TLD emails like @example.test under RFC 6761, reserved fictional phone ranges, reserved test card numbers, and display values like Test User ABC123 that cannot be a real name. That last point is not just hygiene -- it means anyone reading a log, a screenshot, a trace or a support ticket can tell instantly that it is not a person, which removes a whole class of embarrassing incidents. When I genuinely need production-*shaped* data for a performance or bug-reproduction scenario, I take a column allowlist, measure the shape I actually need, and either generate a synthetic population matching those statistics or mask with referential integrity preserved. And the controls are automated, because a written policy is a wish: a CI rule that fails on non-example.test emails and Luhn-valid card numbers in test files, a rule that no test file references a production host, and a nightly janitor that purges test-tagged rows and drops old preview databases.

questions.text: 🔴 Advanced · Must-know — How do you test an LLM feature, given that the output is nondeterministic?
questions.answer: I split the feature into a deterministic shell and a stochastic core. Everything in the shell is ordinary code and gets ordinary unit tests: prompt construction, context budgeting against the window, output parsing, word-budget enforcement, PII redaction, cost accounting. That is often more than half the logic and it is where most real bugs live. The core I evaluate rather than assert on. I never assert on exact output strings -- that is guaranteed flake and it encourages an implementation overfit to one run. I assert on properties that hold across the distribution: every summary within budget, every citation index in range, no ungrounded claim, refusal rate above a threshold across N samples. And for quality I use a versioned evaluation set of a few hundred cases with per-category thresholds, scored by a rubric-based LLM judge that I have validated against a human-labelled gold set at eighty-five percent agreement or better. Two rules make it work operationally: the model id, the prompt version and the eval-set version are a single pinned triple, so nothing is incomparable; and recorded cassettes make the contract tests free and deterministic. I would also say plainly that passing an injection test is evidence, not proof -- the architecture is the real defence, with a deterministic pre-filter, no tools, and output validation.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — How do you test a system with two databases and a saga?
questions.answer: I test the saga as a state machine and assert the *invariants* rather than the choreography, because the interleavings are what matter and there are too many to enumerate. In a transaction-per-test harness the multi-database part is genuinely hard, because the second database cannot join the transaction. My approach is a per-step compensation test: for each step, force the next step to fail and assert that the earlier steps were compensated -- a refunded payment for a failed inventory reservation, a released reservation for a failed payment. Each is a separate test with a real database, using truncate-and-reseed rather than rollback, because a second connection is involved. Then I test the *hard* cases explicitly: a duplicate message arriving after the saga completed, which must be idempotent; an out-of-order message, which must be rejected or deferred; and a step that fails permanently rather than transiently, which must trigger the compensating path rather than the retry path. I use a queue fake that can deliver messages in a scripted order so those tests are deterministic. And I have one test for the case that will actually page someone: the saga is stuck in pending past its timeout with no worker running, and a janitor reclaims it. That path is almost never written, and it is the one that produces manual database surgery at three in the morning.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — How do you test event-driven systems where delivery is at-least-once?
questions.answer: At-least-once means the same event arrives more than once, so the property I test is idempotency: processing an event twice must produce the same state as processing it once. The test is a duplicate-delivery test, and it is the highest-value test in the system. Concretely: publish an event, process it, capture the resulting state; then reset to the pre-event state, deliver the same event *twice* in a row, and assert the state is identical. That catches an entire class of bugs that only appear in production under retry. Then out-of-order. Deliver order.paid before order.created and assert the system either rejects it, defers it, or handles it idempotently -- whichever is your design, but the design must be *written down* and tested. I also test unknown event types, which must be ignored without crashing the consumer, and schema evolution, where a v2 event arrives at a v1 consumer. For the poison-message path, I assert the retry-exhausted behaviour: the message goes to the dead-letter queue after N attempts, with the attempt count and the last error recorded. And I assert the ack/nack contract, because a consumer that acks before committing loses data on a crash, and that is a real bug that only a test with a killed process will find.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — What do you do when the test suite is too slow to be useful?
questions.answer: I measure before I change anything, because the intuition about where time goes is usually wrong. I generate a per-test duration report, sort it, and look at the distribution: is it a few slow tests or everything uniformly slow. If everything is uniformly slow, the cost is per-test setup and I attack the harness -- a shared harness instead of per-file setup, cheaper environment selection so jsdom is not paid for by node tests, a faster transform, and narrower coverage instrumentation. If a few tests dominate, I attack those specifically and usually find a real waitForTimeout or an unbounded retry. Then I move work down tiers, which is the biggest lever: anything an E2E test verifies that a component or integration test can verify moves down, and the payoff is ten to a hundred times per test. Then I reduce flake, which is usually the largest real cost because it is triage time rather than runtime. Then I parallelise: fullyParallel with per-test isolation, shards with duration-based balancing, and separate stages that do not depend on each other running in parallel. And I set budgets -- a suite-duration budget in CI and an alert -- because without one the slow creep back is invisible until the pipeline takes an hour. What I do *not* do is raise timeouts, because every timeout raised to make CI pass is a hidden decision about what your tests actually verify.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — How do you test a design system component library?
questions.answer: The shape is the trophy inverted for a library: most tests should exercise the components through their public API, and the visual and accessibility tiers carry real weight because the components *are* the product. So each component gets: interaction tests through accessible queries, covering keyboard, focus, and state transitions; an accessibility test with axe plus explicit assertions on the roles and relationships the component promises -- a modal traps focus, restores it on close, and has an accessible name; a visual snapshot per state, per theme, per size, generated in a pinned container; and a token test that asserts spacing and colour come from the design tokens rather than hard-coded values, which is how design-system drift starts. The one that teams skip and that I insist on: a composition test that renders the components together in a realistic form or a realistic data table, because components that pass alone and break in composition is the defining failure mode of a component library, and the interaction is usually a focus or a portal or a z-index problem. And a migration test for the version upgrade path, because a design system that cannot be upgraded is a liability.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — What is the difference between mocking, stubbing and faking at the HTTP boundary versus the method boundary, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: The boundary is the whole point. Mocking at the method boundary -- vi.mock('./paymentGateway') or jest.mock -- replaces the adapter, so URL construction, headers, auth, payload serialisation, timeouts, retries and error mapping are all untested. Those are exactly the parts most likely to be wrong, and you have replaced them with a return value you chose. Mocking at the network boundary -- MSW, WireMock, or a real local server -- keeps your adapter under test. You are asserting on the bytes that left the process, which is where the bugs actually are. There is a middle case: stubbing the method but keeping the serialisation. Sometimes you want to test a caller that must handle a provider response, and you cannot produce that response without the provider. Then the highest-fidelity option is a *recorded* real response as a fixture, plus a schema that types the fixture, plus a nightly sandbox test that fails if the real shape drifts. And a Zod schema on the provider's response is the single highest-value line of code in that adapter, because it converts "silently treated an unknown status as success" into a compile-time and runtime failure.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — How do you test a migration?
questions.answer: Three separate things, and I test all three. One: the migration applies cleanly from a *production-shaped* snapshot, not from empty. I take a schema-only dump plus a sample of representative data, apply the migrations, and assert the resulting schema matches expectations. A migration that only works on an empty database will fail in production, and it fails at the worst possible moment. Two: the migration is *reversible*, or the irreversibility is deliberate and documented. I have a test that asserts each migration has a down, or is listed in an explicit irreversible.json with a reason. That file is a design document that gets reviewed. Three: the application is compatible with both sides during the deploy window. This is the one teams miss entirely. I test the old code against the new schema and the new code against the old schema, because for the duration of a rolling deploy both combinations are live. A migration that renames a column will break the previous version of the app, and that is a real outage. And in CI I never use db push or synchronize; the harness always runs the real migration chain, so the migration path is exercised on every single integration run.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — How do you test caching?
questions.answer: Caching has three independent behaviours and each needs its own test. First, does it hit: after a first request populates the cache, a second identical request must not reach the database. I assert that by counting queries or by spying on the data source, not by asserting on a response header, because the header is an implementation detail that lies. Second, does it invalidate correctly. This is where the bugs are. I test every write path that should invalidate -- update, delete, and any bulk operation -- and assert the next read sees the new value. I also test the *selective* case: invalidating a user's cache must not evict a different user's, which is a real bug in tag-based invalidation. Third, the failure modes: TTL expiry, an eviction storm under memory pressure, and a cache stampede, where N concurrent requests all miss and all hit the database. For the stampede I test that a single-flight or lock mechanism reduces concurrent origin requests to one, using a fake that counts simultaneous misses and asserts the count is bounded. I also test the serialisation round trip explicitly, because a cached object that was serialised and deserialised must behave identically -- a Date that became a string, a class instance that became a plain object. That bug is invisible in development with an in-process cache and appears the moment you enable Redis.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — How do you test a feature behind a feature flag?
questions.answer: I treat the flag as a dimension, not a state, so I test the matrix. Every test that touches a flagged code path runs with the flag on and off, and asserts the *correct* behaviour in each, not merely that nothing crashed. Off should give the old behaviour; on should give the new; and there must be a defined state for "user has seen neither", because partial rollout means most users are in that state and it is rarely specified. I test the three operational properties too. The default: what happens if the flag service is unreachable? The answer must be a defined, safe fallback, and I test it by making the flag client throw. The evaluation: I test that the flag is evaluated once per request rather than per render, because per-render evaluation is a performance bug and an inconsistency bug. And the kill switch: the test asserts that setting the flag to false restores the old path *without a deploy*, which is the whole reason the flag exists. Structurally, I insist flags are read through one typed accessor, so flag('new-checkout') is the only way to read one. String literals scattered through the code are how flags become un-removable, and un-removable flags are the actual cost.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — How do you test optimistic UI updates and rollback?
questions.answer: Optimistic UI is where the interesting failures live, because there are four distinct states and a naive test only covers the first. The four: the optimistic state immediately after the user acts, before any response; the confirmed state; the *rolled-back* state if the mutation fails; and the *reconciled* state if the server's response differs from what you assumed. I test all four, and the last two are the ones that are usually missing. For rollback, I assert three things: the UI returned to the previous value, the user was *told* -- a status message, not a silent revert, because a value that silently changes back is a bug report waiting to happen -- and no partial state remains, so a list item is not left as a duplicate or an orphan. For reconciliation, I have the server return a value different from the optimistic one -- a normalised name, a recomputed total, a server-assigned id -- and assert the UI ends up showing the *server's* value. That is a real class of bug and no happy-path test finds it. The test mechanics: the mutation is slow enough to observe the optimistic state, which means a controllable deferred in the mock, not a sleep. And I use a fake timer or an explicit deferred so the intermediate state is asserted deterministically rather than raced.

questions.text: ⚫ Expert · Nice-to-have — What is your philosophy on deleting tests?
questions.answer: Deleting a test is a claim: that the behaviour it verified is now verified elsewhere, or is no longer required. Both are legitimate, and both need evidence. So the default is not deletion, it is *relocation* -- moving a test down a tier when a cheaper tier can carry it -- and only deletion when the behaviour is genuinely gone. Three things make a test a deletion candidate. It duplicates another test with no additional signal. It asserts an implementation detail that no longer exists, and the behaviour is covered by a behavioural test. Or it was added to chase a coverage number and mutation testing shows it kills no mutants. Three rules I hold. You may not delete a test in the same PR that changes the behaviour, unless the replacement test is in that PR and named in the description. You may not delete a test to make a flaky suite green -- you quarantine it with a ticket and an owner. And every deletion must be justified by evidence: a mutation score comparison, or a pointer to the test that now covers the behaviour. The metric I actually watch is *escape rate by tier*: bugs that reached production and which tier should have caught them. A tier that is quietly full of deleted tests shows up there first, which is a much better signal than test count.

practice.title: PHASE 9 RAPID-FIRE
items: 🟢 describe vs it? -- describe groups related tests and owns scoped hooks; it is one test with one behaviour. test is an alias for it.
🟢 expect alone does nothing? -- Correct. It is lazy; nothing is verified until a matcher runs. Use expect.assertions(n) to prove you asserted.
🟢 toBe vs toEqual? -- toBe is Object.is (identity, NaN equal, -0 not); toEqual is deep structural and ignores undefined properties.
🟢 toStrictEqual adds what? -- Class/prototype checks and undefined-sparseness checks that toEqual skips.
🟢 Jest hook order? -- outer beforeAll -> inner beforeAll -> outer beforeEach -> inner beforeEach -> test -> inner afterEach -> outer afterEach -> inner afterAll -> outer afterAll.
🟢 Does beforeAll run per test? -- No. Once per worker per file.
🟡 it.only risk? -- Silently skips every other test in the run. Block it in ESLint and set forbidOnly: true in CI.
🟡 Best negative assertion? -- expect(spy).not.toHaveBeenCalled() and friends -- asserting that something *did not* happen is the highest-value class in unit tests.
🟡 Why userEvent over fireEvent? -- It dispatches the full event sequence (pointer, focus, key, input) and respects disabled/pointer-events, so it reproduces real failures.
🟡 Why findBy* over getBy* for async? -- findBy* retries; getBy* throws immediately. Also use waitFor, not waitForTimeout.
🟡 expect.hasAssertions()? -- Fails the test if zero assertions ran, catching a silently short-circuited path in a heavily-mocked test.
🔴 clearMocks vs resetMocks vs restoreMocks? -- clear resets calls only; reset also wipes implementations (breaks jest.fn(impl)); restore restores spied originals.
🔴 Why did resetMocks: true break a suite? -- It removes factory implementations, so configured mocks return undefined and failures surface far from the cause.
🟢 Vite: what is vi? -- Vitest's API object: vi.fn, vi.spyOn, vi.mock, vi.useFakeTimers, vi.stubEnv, vi.advanceTimersByTime.
🟢 Why is Vitest faster? -- Vite's esbuild transform and native ESM graph instead of Babel/ts-jest compiling to CJS, plus a warm server for watch mode.
🟡 Vitest's vi.hoisted()? -- Creates a value initialised before hoisted vi.mock factories run, solving "mock out of variable scope".
🔴 Vitest vs Jest fake timer difference? -- Vitest fakes more APIs by default (performance, queueMicrotask, nextTick); narrow with toFake.
🟡 clearMocks: true in Vitest? -- vi.clearAllMocks() in config clears call history before every test.
🔴 Why does a test hang only in Vitest? -- Fake timers faked the microtask pump, or a dependency is not inlined so its ESM interop differs. Use advanceTimersByTimeAsync and check server.deps.inline.
🟡 AAA expand? -- Arrange, Act, Assert. One Act per test; the Act is the smallest possible call.
🟡 Test factory vs builder? -- Factory: one call with an overridable object. Builder: fluent chaining when many fields vary across tests.
🔴 When does a factory become harmful? -- When it can build states the real system forbids, becoming a second, wrong domain model. Derive its types from production types.
🟢 Property-based library? -- fast-check. fc.assert(fc.property(...)); prints a shrunk counterexample plus a reproducible seed.
🟢 Round-trip property? -- decode(encode(x)) === x. The first property to reach for on codecs, serialisers and URL builders.
🟡 Conservation property? -- sum(parts) === whole. Essential for payment splitting, where a lost cent is a real defect.
🔴 Property tests flaky in CI? -- Almost never flaky; they find real bugs. Fix the seed's counterexample as a deterministic regression test.
🟢 TDD cycle? -- Red, Green, Refactor. Confirm red fails for the *expected* reason; green in the simplest way; refactor only while green.
🟡 Why hardcode in the green step? -- To prove the harness and assertion work, isolating a test failure from an implementation failure.
🔴 Where does TDD not pay? -- Exploratory spikes, UI layout work, throwaway prototypes, fixed-deadline throwaway code, and legacy code needing characterisation tests.
🟢 Coverage metrics? -- Statement/line, branch, function. Istanbul is AST-based and precise; V8 is fast and coarser.
🔴 Biggest coverage trap? -- The 100% gate, achieved with toBeDefined() assertions. It optimises the number, not the defect rate.
🟡 Diff coverage? -- Gates that *changed* lines are covered, comparing against the base branch. Far better than an absolute global threshold.
🟡 Snapshot vs explicit assertions? -- Snapshots detect change; explicit assertions detect correctness. Use both.
🔴 Never do this with snapshots? -- -u in CI; snapshotting component DOM; leaving obsolete entries to rot.
🟡 Serialisers fix what? -- Nondeterministic values: dates, uuids, ids, hashes, Errors, object key order, Set/Map iteration.
🟢 advanceTimersByTime vs ...Async? -- Sync fires callbacks only; async also drains the microtask queue. Async is what async code needs.
🔴 Four ways async tests lie about time? -- Not awaiting; real time; sync timer advance; leaked timers/handles.
🟡 Injected Clock vs fake timers? -- Injected clock for your own code always; fake timers only for third-party code you cannot change.
🟢 RTL query priority? -- role (+name), label, placeholder, text, alt, testid. Testid is a last resort.
🟡 Why role queries? -- They assert the user's contract, so a component you cannot query by role is usually one a screen reader user cannot use.
