topics.description: AAA pattern within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: AAA
Arrange helpers -- functions that build the precondition. Their job is to make the *only* thing that varies visible in the test body.

Test data factories / builders -- parameterised constructors that produce valid-by-default objects, overridable field by field, with relational integrity (a customer() that yields a customer with a defaultCard referencing *that* customer's id, not a hard-coded UUID).
One Act per test. Two acts means two behaviours; if the second depends on the first's state, you cannot assert the first in isolation.
The Act is the smallest possible call. Act on one function, not on a chain that also parses, validates and persists.

Assertions read as sentences. expect(result.totalCents).toBe(4200) is a sentence. expect(result).toEqual({...17 fields...}) is a change-detector: it fails on every irrelevant field addition and buries the real assertion.
Arrange helpers must be pure and default-rich. A helper that requires 6 arguments is not a helper; make 5 of them default.
Factories must be deterministic. Fixed IDs, fixed timestamps via an injected clock, no Math.random() -- otherwise failures are unreproducible and you cannot use snapshot diffing.
Factories live in test code, not production code. Exporting createUser from src and calling it in tests means your production bundle contains test-only code paths.
Override, don't mutate. Builders return new objects; a helper that mutates a shared constant produces order-dependent tests.

keyConcepts: TDD
Red
*Failure mode:* a test that fails because the function does not exist yet is fine. A test that fails because your import is wrong is not -- you have learned nothing.
*Failure mode:* writing 12 red tests before any green. You have written a design document; you lose the incremental feedback that makes TDD valuable.
Green
*Failure mode:* the classic "I wrote the real implementation in the first green." You skip the "does my test work at all?" check and can end up with a test that passes for the wrong reason.
Refactor

*Failure mode:* refactoring without a net, or refactoring so aggressively you change the public contract while the test stays green (only possible if your test was weak -- which TDD's discipline should have prevented).
*Failure mode:* "refactor" as a euphemism for "rewrite". If behaviour changes, that is a new green, and you need a new red.

topics.title: Testing async code and timers
topics.description: Testing async code and timers within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: The test finishes before the async work does -- you assert on a promise that has not resolved; await is missing or on the wrong promise. Symptom: intermittent "expected undefined", or a test that passes even when the code is broken.
Real time is slower than the test's patience -- the test uses a real setTimeout(50) and CI is loaded. Symptom: the classic "works locally, fails in CI".

Fake time is advanced but the microtask queue is not -- advanceTimersByTime (synchronous) fires the timer callback but any await inside it is queued as a microtask that never runs before your assertion. Symptom: the assertion sees the state from *before* the callback completed. This is the single most common timer bug.

The system under test schedules a timeout but the test never flushes it, or flushes it and leaks it -- the test finishes with a pending timer, and Jest prints "A worker process has failed to exit gracefully" or the next test is affected. Symptom: open handles, "Cannot log after tests are done", memory growth.
The four lie-modes, matched to their fixes, in one table
Tooling that finds these lies for you
When fake timers vs injected clock
Fake timers when the code under test is *third-party* or uses globals directly and you cannot change it (a debounce inside a library, a setInterval in a component you do not own).

Injected clock for your own code, always. It is faster, parallel-safe, has no microtask subtleties, produces better failures, and works identically in the browser. It is also the only approach that scales to *ordering* tests.
Never fake timers globally for a whole test file that also contains pure synchronous tests -- you gain nothing and lose the ability to test real async I/O in the same file.

Fake timers couple your tests to the *shape* of the code (it must use globals) and to the runner's timer implementation. Vitest's @sinonjs/fake-timers defaults differ from Jest's, so tests are not always portable.

Injecting a clock is a design commitment: every module needs the port threaded through. That is a cost paid once and refunded forever, and it is the right investment in any system with a time rule (sessions, retries, billing, caches, jobs).

keyConcepts: "A unit is a function." -- the smallest testable thing. Too small: it produces tests that assert implementation facts and break on every refactor.
"A unit is a class." -- inherited from JUnit/Java. Better: it introduces a boundary that matches the design vocabulary of the codebase.

"A unit is a module/file." -- the practical JavaScript/TypeScript definition: one test file per source file, everything imported from outside is a substitute. This is what most teams mean and what Vitest/Jest give you structurally.

"A unit is a behaviour, not a code unit." 🟡 -- the *behavioural* definition. A unit is one observable rule the system promises (e.g. "an expired token cannot be redeemed"), regardless of how many functions cooperate to implement it. Tests are named after behaviours, and a test file may or may not map to a source file.
The three questions that dissolve 90% of unit/integration arguments
*Can I run this with zero network, zero disk and zero database?* If yes, it is a unit test. If no, it is at least an integration test.

*Would this test still pass if I rewrote the implementation with different internals but identical observable behaviour?* If yes, it is testing behaviour (good). If no, it is testing implementation (a bug waiting for a refactor).

*Who owns the thing I am substituting?* If I stub something I own, I can change it freely. If I stub something a third party owns, you are writing a test that breaks on their patch release -- a vendor-coupled test, and it belongs in the integration tier or nowhere.
Runnable code -- the canonical shape of a good unit test
The logic has *branches worth enumerating* (pricing, permissions, state machines, parsers, retries, encoders).
The logic is *pure or nearly pure* -- the best case, and worth architecting for.
You intend to *refactor aggressively* and need a safety net that survives the refactor.

expect is lazy and assertion-free until a matcher runs. expect(1) does nothing. A test with no matcher passes vacuously and is worse than no test -- this is the "vacuous test" anti-pattern.

Matcher catalogue that you actually use: toBe (Object.is -- beware NaN and -0), toEqual (deep structural, ignores undefined properties), toStrictEqual (also checks class/undefined sparseness), toMatchObject (subset), toContain/toContainEqual (arrays, strings, sets), toHaveLength, toHaveProperty (dot or array path for deep access), toBeCloseTo (float), toThrow/toThrowError, toHaveBeenCalled/toHaveBeenCalledWith/toHaveBeenCalledTimes/toHaveBeenNthCalledWith/toHaveReturnedWith, toMatchSnapshot/toMatchInlineSnapshot, toSatisfy, .not, .resolves/.rejects.

Hooks are scoped, not global. beforeEach in an outer describe runs before every test in *every* nested describe. Order is: outer beforeAll -> inner beforeAll -> outer beforeEach -> inner beforeEach -> test -> inner afterEach -> outer afterEach -> inner afterAll -> outer afterAll.

Fake timers replace Date, setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, process.nextTick, queueMicrotask, and (in modern Jest) performance.now. jest.useFakeTimers() then jest.advanceTimersByTime(ms) / jest.runAllTimers() / jest.runOnlyPendingTimers() / jest.setSystemTime(date). await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(ms) yields to the microtask queue so promises can settle -- using the *sync* variant with async code is one of the most common hangs in the ecosystem.

test.concurrent runs tests in a file concurrently; any shared module state immediately becomes a race. Treat as a sharp tool.
Environments: jsdom, node, jest-environment-jsdom (must be installed separately in Jest 28+), testEnvironmentOptions: { url: 'https://app.test' }, customExportConditions for package resolution.

Jest's transform pipeline is its main tax. Babel or ts-jest compiling every file per worker, then a jsdom instance per test file, is why Jest suites take 30-120s on projects where Vitest takes 4s. @swc/jest recovers most of it by swapping Babel for the Rust-based SWC compiler.

clearMocks/resetMocks semantics are a classic footgun. resetMocks: true clears factory implementations passed to jest.fn(impl), turning your configured mock into a no-op that returns undefined, and the failure surfaces 200 lines away in some unrelated assertion.

Mock with verification -- only when *the call itself* is the behaviour under test (e.g. "publishes an order.created event to Kafka with this payload").
Total mock of a system boundary in a unit test -- the smell; belongs in the integration tier with MSW or Testcontainers.
Runnable code -- all five doubles, side by side, in one test file
Fakes that pay for themselves
Mock -- when the interaction with a boundary (message published, email sent, third-party API called) *is* the contract, and you do not want a network call. Otherwise it is a liability.
Stub -- when a return value is merely an input; never assert on the stub's calls.
Spy -- for logging, metrics, caching layers, and to assert "did not write to the audit log".

topics.title: AAA pattern, arrange helpers, and test data factories
topics.description: AAA pattern, arrange helpers, and test data factories within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: AAA
Arrange helpers -- functions that build the precondition. Their job is to make the *only* thing that varies visible in the test body.

Test data factories / builders -- parameterised constructors that produce valid-by-default objects, overridable field by field, with relational integrity (a customer() that yields a customer with a defaultCard referencing *that* customer's id, not a hard-coded UUID).
One Act per test. Two acts means two behaviours; if the second depends on the first's state, you cannot assert the first in isolation.
The Act is the smallest possible call. Act on one function, not on a chain that also parses, validates and persists.

Assertions read as sentences. expect(result.totalCents).toBe(4200) is a sentence. expect(result).toEqual({...17 fields...}) is a change-detector: it fails on every irrelevant field addition and buries the real assertion.
Arrange helpers must be pure and default-rich. A helper that requires 6 arguments is not a helper; make 5 of them default.
Factories must be deterministic. Fixed IDs, fixed timestamps via an injected clock, no Math.random() -- otherwise failures are unreproducible and you cannot use snapshot diffing.
Factories live in test code, not production code. Exporting createUser from src and calling it in tests means your production bundle contains test-only code paths.
Override, don't mutate. Builders return new objects; a helper that mutates a shared constant produces order-dependent tests.

topics.title: Pure functions and property-based testing
topics.description: Pure functions and property-based testing within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: Property-based testing (PBT)
Runnable code -- fast-check over a money/pricing domain
Authoring cost. Generators require thought about domain invariants (filter for cross-field constraints). Budget 2-5x a single example test.
Debugging cost is lower, paradoxically, because the counterexample is minimal and the seed is printed -- you can reproduce with fc.assert(prop, { seed: 1234 }).
Flakiness risk from unseeded randomness. Always fix the seed in CI, or use fc.configureGlobal({ seed: 0 }); a "flaky" PBT failure is almost always a real bug the previous run happened not to find.
Smaller numRuns in CI for slow properties, and a separate nightly job with numRuns: 50_000 to mine deeper.
Persist the failing seed to CI artefacts so a developer can reproduce locally; keep a property-failures/ directory of counterexamples promoted to deterministic regression tests.
Run PBT in a dedicated test:property script; it is the slowest tier and does not need to gate every commit.
Combine with fuzzing for parsers: fc.string() with a large maxLength and a byte-level arbitrary (fc.uint8Array) gets close for codec code.
For crypto, use a known-answer test (KAT) from a published vector *in addition to* round-trip properties; round-trip alone will not catch a key-order mistake.
Asserting a property the type system already guarantees -- wasted budget.
Properties that are trivially true because of the implementation (asserting x === x).

topics.title: TDD: red, green, refactor, and where it actually pays off
topics.description: TDD: red, green, refactor, and where it actually pays off within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: TDD
Red
*Failure mode:* a test that fails because the function does not exist yet is fine. A test that fails because your import is wrong is not -- you have learned nothing.
*Failure mode:* writing 12 red tests before any green. You have written a design document; you lose the incremental feedback that makes TDD valuable.
Green
*Failure mode:* the classic "I wrote the real implementation in the first green." You skip the "does my test work at all?" check and can end up with a test that passes for the wrong reason.
Refactor

*Failure mode:* refactoring without a net, or refactoring so aggressively you change the public contract while the test stays green (only possible if your test was weak -- which TDD's discipline should have prevented).
*Failure mode:* "refactor" as a euphemism for "rewrite". If behaviour changes, that is a new green, and you need a new red.
Refactor-only-with-tests (the honest admission)
Runnable code -- one full cycle, showing the throwaway green
When TDD pays off vs not

topics.title: Coverage: what it measures, what it misses, and the coverage traps
topics.description: Coverage: what it measures, what it misses, and the coverage traps within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: Code coverage

Assertions. A test that calls a function and asserts nothing is 100% coverage of that function. Coverage cannot see that expect is missing. The mitigations are expect.assertions(n) and expect.hasAssertions(), not coverage.
Correctness of expectations. 100% coverage with wrong assertions is the worst possible state: full confidence, zero signal.
Behaviour outside the executed paths. Mutation testing exists precisely to measure this (9.4.4).
Interleavings and concurrency. A race in a message consumer has 0% "missing lines" and a real bug.
The system. Coverage of unit tests says nothing about whether the deployed configuration, DNS, or migration is right.
Test quality per line. Two tests can hit the same line; the second may assert nothing.
Timing/performance/memory. Never measured by coverage.
The coverage traps, enumerated

The 100% gate. A codebase at 100% coverage with vacuous assertions is less trustworthy than one at 60% with strong property tests. 100% is almost always achieved by adding it('returns a value', () => { expect(f(1)).toBeDefined() }).
Coverage of generated code. Instrumenting dist/, node_modules, .d.ts, barrel index.ts re-exports, and framework glue distorts every number. Exclude them explicitly.
Coverage of the *test* files themselves. Always exclude *.spec.ts; otherwise your metric rewards writing more test lines.

topics.title: Snapshot testing: the good use, the bad use, and obsolete-snapshot rot
topics.description: Snapshot testing: the good use, the bad use, and obsolete-snapshot rot within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: Serialisation must be deterministic. JSON.stringify is insertion-order dependent; object keys from a Map, Set, Promise.all completion order, Date, and class instances all serialise unpredictably. You almost always need a snapshot serializer that normalises: sorted keys, replaced ids/uuids/dates/timestamps, truncated hashes, sorted arrays where order is not semantically meaningful.

propertyMatchers (Jest) and matchers (Vitest) let you ignore noisy fields, e.g. expect.addSnapshotSerializer({ test: (v) => typeof v === 'string' && /^[0-9a-f]{24}$/.test(v), print: () => 'HexString' }).

-u is the most dangerous flag in the toolchain. It rewrites the artefact without asking. A reviewer must read snapshot diffs as carefully as code diffs -- a *process* requirement, not a technical one.
Obsolete snapshots (no test references them any more) linger. In CI you must set updateSnapshot: 'none' and fail on obsolete entries. Unreferenced .snap entries should be deleted, not left to rot.

Snapshots are not reviewable when huge. A 4000-line .snap diff is not reviewed; it is rubber-stamped. The moment the snapshot is too big to read, it has lost its value and should be replaced by explicit assertions.
Vitest's obsolete-snapshot handling and a CI guard
The rot-prevention protocol (this is the part most teams skip)
Small and inline by default. If a snapshot does not fit in a PR diff you would actually read, it does not go in.
Serializers cover every volatile field, and you add a serializer *the moment* a snapshot fails for a non-behavioural reason. This keeps the "review noise" ratio near zero.

Explicit assertions for the things that matter. Snapshot = "everything else did not change". Then add 3-5 targeted expects for invariants that must hold (auth required, this field present, this status code). Snapshots detect *change*; explicit assertions detect *correctness*. You need both.
-u is a code review artefact. A PR whose diff is 900 lines of .snap change is a signal to add a serializer or an explicit assertion, not to approve.
Delete on removal. When you delete a test, run -u and commit the deletion of the orphaned entry. Configure the runner to fail on obsolete entries.

wrongAnswers: a single value you can assert precisely, error messages, business-critical numeric results, component DOM markup, anything a human must read to be useful, and anything with more than a handful of volatile fields.

topics.title: Async code and timers: the four ways tests lie about time
topics.description: Async code and timers: the four ways tests lie about time within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: The test finishes before the async work does -- you assert on a promise that has not resolved; await is missing or on the wrong promise. Symptom: intermittent "expected undefined", or a test that passes even when the code is broken.
Real time is slower than the test's patience -- the test uses a real setTimeout(50) and CI is loaded. Symptom: the classic "works locally, fails in CI".

Fake time is advanced but the microtask queue is not -- advanceTimersByTime (synchronous) fires the timer callback but any await inside it is queued as a microtask that never runs before your assertion. Symptom: the assertion sees the state from *before* the callback completed. This is the single most common timer bug.

The system under test schedules a timeout but the test never flushes it, or flushes it and leaks it -- the test finishes with a pending timer, and Jest prints "A worker process has failed to exit gracefully" or the next test is affected. Symptom: open handles, "Cannot log after tests are done", memory growth.
The four lie-modes, matched to their fixes, in one table
Tooling that finds these lies for you
When fake timers vs injected clock
Fake timers when the code under test is *third-party* or uses globals directly and you cannot change it (a debounce inside a library, a setInterval in a component you do not own).

Injected clock for your own code, always. It is faster, parallel-safe, has no microtask subtleties, produces better failures, and works identically in the browser. It is also the only approach that scales to *ordering* tests.
Never fake timers globally for a whole test file that also contains pure synchronous tests -- you gain nothing and lose the ability to test real async I/O in the same file.

Fake timers couple your tests to the *shape* of the code (it must use globals) and to the runner's timer implementation. Vitest's @sinonjs/fake-timers defaults differ from Jest's, so tests are not always portable.

Injecting a clock is a design commitment: every module needs the port threaded through. That is a cost paid once and refunded forever, and it is the right investment in any system with a time rule (sessions, retries, billing, caches, jobs).

topics.title: React component testing philosophy: implementation details vs user-visible behavior
topics.description: React component testing philosophy: implementation details vs user-visible behavior within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: Component testing
The three testable layers of a component, and where to draw the line
Behaviour (assert here). What the user can do and observe: enabled/disabled, visible text, validation messages, focus movement, error announcements, aria-* state, the callback payload.
Structure (assert sparingly). Only when the structure *is* the requirement: a <table> with <th scope> for a data grid, a <fieldset>+<legend> group, a modal's role="dialog" and aria-modal.
Implementation (never assert). Hook call order, useState internals, useMemo dependency arrays, class names, conditional rendering branches, prop identity.
What to mock in a component test -- the narrow line

Mock: network (MSW, at the boundary -- see 9.2.6), the *parent* (render the component in isolation with a fake onSubmit), time and randomness, and heavy third-party widgets (a chart, a map, a payment iframe) where the test's subject is the surrounding layout, not the widget.

Do not mock: your own hooks (useCart, useUser), your own presentational children, your own validators. Mocking them means the test cannot find a bug in them, and you end up with 40 tests that all pass while the app is broken. If a hook needs mocking to be testable, extract the logic into a pure function and test that directly.
Do not mock: react, react-dom, the router provider, or @tanstack/react-query (MSW at the network layer tests the real query hook, which is what production uses).
Async component testing: the four things you must get right
Use findBy* (or await waitFor) for anything that arrives asynchronously. getBy* on async content throws immediately.

Use userEvent, not fireEvent, for user interactions. userEvent dispatches the full event sequence (pointerdown, mousedown, focus, input, keyup) and honours disabled, readonly, and pointer-events. fireEvent.change skips half of it and will pass when the real interaction fails.

topics.title: Hook testing and testing custom hooks
topics.description: Hook testing and testing custom hooks within Unit Testing.
keyConcepts: Wrap state mutations you perform yourself in act: act(() => result.current.setOpen(true)), act(() => window.dispatchEvent(new Event('online'))).
Never wrap render in act -- RTL already does.
waitFor beats act(async () => { await sleep(50) }); prefer findBy* for DOM and waitFor for hook state.

"An update to X inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)" usually means something outside React (a timer, a promise, an event listener) is calling a setter. Either the code should be restructured, or the test should act around the trigger.
The subscribe/cleanup contract -- the highest-value hook test
The "logic in a hook" anti-pattern and its fix

renderHook tests are close to unit tests but not quite: they need a DOM (or react-test-renderer/a no-DOM renderer), they are subject to React's concurrent rendering rules, and they cannot be run in a pure node environment. This is why extracting logic into pure functions is strictly better where you can.
Hook tests couple to the hook's API, so a signature change breaks them -- but that is a *good* coupling, because the API *is* the contract.

Effect timing is a source of frustration: useEffect does not run during render, and in StrictMode it runs twice in development. Test with renderHook in the default (non-StrictMode) test entry point, and enable StrictMode selectively in one test to assert idempotent mount/unmount.

renderHook is React-only. Svelte, Vue and Solid need different harnesses (@testing-library/svelte, mount from @vue/test-utils, createRoot from solid-js/web); the *philosophy* transfers, the API does not.
Standardise on renderHook and export a renderHookWithProviders from your test utilities, so every hook test gets the real providers.
Enforce the "logic out of the hook" rule by convention and review: hooks over 40 lines of branching get a *.reducer.ts beside them.

keyConcepts: Seeding
Why transaction-per-test usually works and when it does not
your code under test commits inside the test (a prisma.$transaction nested call, a separate connection, a COMMIT in raw SQL) -- then the test's rollback cannot undo it;
your code uses two connections concurrently (a queue worker polling while the request runs) -- the worker's changes are not in your transaction;
you need to test READ COMMITTED vs SERIALIZABLE behaviour with two actors;
the code uses LISTEN/NOTIFY, advisory locks, or advisory-based coordination across connections.
Seeders: minimal, relational, and derived from production types
Isolation patterns for the cases transaction-per-test cannot cover
No data at all when the test creates what it needs inline (the best option; no shared fixture, no cross-test coupling).
Factory-per-test for one or two entities.
Seeding helpers for three or more tests needing the same graph (e.g. a user with a saved card and a past order).

Bulk seeding (createMany, generate_series in raw SQL) for pagination, performance, and load tests. Use raw SQL for >10 000 rows; createMany is still one statement per batch and is slow beyond a few thousand.

topics.title: Service mocking
topics.description: Service mocking within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Anti-patterns, with the specific failure each causes
The four verification mechanisms that keep you honest
Contract-test the double. Write one suite that runs against both the fake and the real implementation.
Use recorded fixtures from the real system. For outbound third-party clients, record a real response once and assert the fake reproduces it.
Type the double as the real port and forbid divergence.

Assert the negative space. For every mock, assert the paths that the mock would *not* let you reach: timeouts, cancellation, malformed responses, partial responses, HTTP 429, HTTP 5xx, connection reset.
"Do not mock the thing you own to test the thing you own."

Mocks are fast and precise; reality is slow and messy. The cost of a mock is that it is a hypothesis. The cost of reality is a 3-second test, a container, and a schema you have to keep in sync. You pay the second cost exactly once per dependency, in the contract test, and then you get the first cost everywhere else.

A contract test is a real, ongoing cost that is easy to forget. It is, however, dramatically cheaper than the incident it prevents ("we assumed the provider returns 200 on a soft decline; it returns 202 with status: pending").

A mock-heavy suite is a knowledge transfer problem. The next engineer must reconstruct the real behaviour from the mocks. Where you can, prefer MSW so that the real adapter code is the thing being described.
Mocking your own pure function, so the logic is never tested.
A mock whose return value is narrower than reality, so your real serialisation/deserialisation path is never executed.

topics.description: Error simulation within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Error simulation
Database failure simulation
Observability assertions -- the failure path you almost never test
Testing partial failure in a batch
The reliability-pattern tests you should always have
When to focus on failure paths

Failure tests are the highest-value and least-maintained tests in most suites. They tend to be written once during an incident and then rot as the code changes shape. Budget for rewriting them when you refactor the client.
Simulating real socket-level failures requires real servers, which is slower and less portable than MSW. Use MSW for protocol-level failures and a real net.Server for transport-level ones.

Injecting timeouts via delay('infinite') in MSW is real time. A 1500ms timeout test takes 1.5s. With 20 such tests that is 30 seconds. Consider delay(10) with a client timeout of 5ms for speed, accepting that it tests the timeout logic rather than the exact duration, and keep one test with realistic numbers.
Killing a database backend is genuinely disruptive -- it will fail *other* tests running in parallel. Only do it in a dedicated, serialised suite.
Testing only the 4xx paths, because they are easy to trigger with a mock, and never the 5xx/timeout/reset paths.
Asserting only the status code on the error path, not the error code, the log, and the metric.

topics.description: MSW within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Mock Service Worker (MSW)

Request handlers (declarative, default). http.get('/api/user', () => HttpResponse.json({...})) registered on a setupServer instance. Used in tests and in node (Vitest/Jest). Handlers are matched in reverse registration order (last registered wins), with optional path params, wildcards, and predicates.

Storybook-style handlers (in-browser, for development). msw-storybook-addon lets you define handlers once and use them both as a mock backend for Storybook and as the test backend, guaranteeing that stories exercise the same contract as tests.
Handler design: base handlers plus per-test overrides
Cassettes / record-and-replay
Your outbound adapter's behaviour is now genuinely tested -- the big win. URL construction, headers, auth, serialisation, timeouts, retries, and error mapping all run for real.

It is a fake server, so the provider's real behaviour is still unknown. MSW proves you speak the protocol you *think* the provider speaks. Contract tests (9.2.7) and periodic sandbox runs close the remaining gap.

onUnhandledRequest: 'error' is a setting you should make and keep. It turns "my handler has the wrong URL" into an immediate, obvious failure instead of a mysterious 404 from the wrong place. In development/Storybook, use 'bypass'.

Service Worker mode has gotchas: it requires a secure context (localhost counts), it can serve stale handlers until unregistered, and in Playwright you must route MSW's worker script or disable SW. In Node, @mswjs/interceptors patches http/fetch/XHR, which does not intercept a raw net.Socket write.

Latency simulation with delay() is the fastest way to write a debounce/spinner test -- and also the fastest way to introduce a real-time flake if you forget it is real. Prefer advanceTimersByTimeAsync with fake timers, or keep the delay well under the test timeout.
Keep handlers in one module, imported by tests, Storybook, and the dev server. Single source of truth for the backend shape is the entire value.
Generate handlers from your OpenAPI/GraphQL schema where you can (msw-openapi-har or openapi-msw), so a schema change breaks the handler set rather than silently serving stale shapes.

topics.title: Testcontainers
topics.description: Testcontainers within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Testcontainers
Container start. A container image is started with a specific configuration (image tag or digest, env, command, port bindings, mounted volumes, a tmpfs for speed).

Wait strategy. The container is not ready when docker run returns. Testcontainers uses a *wait strategy* -- waitForListeningPort(), wait.forLogMessage(), wait.forHealthCheck(), or a custom wait -- and blocks until the dependency is genuinely usable.
Connection details. getMappedPort(5432) and getHost() produce a connection URL. Because ports are dynamic, every test file must read the URL from the container, never hardcode 5432.
Reuse. withReuse() keeps the container alive between runs (a huge local speedup) and requires opt-in (testcontainers.reuse.enable=true in ~/.testcontainers.properties).
Teardown. Ryuk (the resource reaper container) monitors the JVM/Node process and kills orphans when it dies, so a crashed run does not leak containers.
The "system under test in a container" pattern

Requires a working Docker daemon. In restricted CI, in some corporate networks, and on machines without Docker, this is a hard blocker. Have a fallback: an env var pointing at a managed Postgres (TEST_DATABASE_URL), and a documented "no Docker? use this" path.
Startup cost. 1-5s per container, serialised. globalSetup amortises it across the whole run. Reuse eliminates it locally.
Resource use. Each container needs memory; 8 workers each starting a container will exhaust a laptop. Start once per process, not per file.

Cleanup is best-effort. A hard kill (CI runner OOM) can leak containers. Ryuk handles the common case; add a CI step docker ps -aq --filter "label=org.testcontainers=true" | xargs -r docker rm -f for safety.
Image drift. postgres:16 moves under you. Pin a minor (16.4) or a digest, and consider a nightly job against the newest minor to catch deprecations before your users do.

topics.description: Contract testing (Pact) within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Runnable code -- the consumer side (Pact-JS / pact-js)
Runnable code -- the provider side (verification)
Provider state is where contracts rot
Matcher strictness is the design decision that matters most in CDC

You get decoupling and a real change-warning mechanism; you pay for it in ceremony: a broker, a state-setup endpoint, per-field matcher decisions, and a provider verification job. For two teams this is a clear win; for twenty services it is an operational platform you must staff.

Pacts are *tolerant* by default: unlisted fields are ignored and extra requests cause a failure only if you configure it. This is right for additive change and wrong for accidental behaviour change. Use allowUnexpectedRequests: false if you want strictness, accepting that it will flag benign additions.

Canary deployments solve the "which pact version do I verify?" problem: the provider verifies against the consumer version that will actually be deployed (or soon will be), which is what consumerVersionSelectors with deployedOrRelease gives you.

State setup is real work and a real maintenance burden. A state that takes 20 lines of seeding is a state nobody will add, and a missing state means a failed verification, which means teams learn to --skip verification, which kills the whole mechanism.
A generated mock cannot be the source of truth for the provider's own tests. Pact verifies the provider; it does not improve the provider's test suite.
Run provider verification in CI before deploy, and block the pipeline on failure. A green main branch that has not been verified against canary consumer pacts is a broken gate.
Tag consumer pacts: main (the current stable), prod (what is deployed), and feature branches. Then the provider can ask the broker "what am I about to break?"
Use the PactFlow (or PactSafe-style) CI integration so the Slack notification and the PR comment come for free.

Factories must be deterministic. Fixed IDs, fixed timestamps via an injected clock, no Math.random() -- otherwise failures are unreproducible and you cannot use snapshot diffing.
Factories live in test code, not production code. Exporting createUser from src and calling it in tests means your production bundle contains test-only code paths.
Override, don't mutate. Builders return new objects; a helper that mutates a shared constant produces order-dependent tests.

topics.title: What integration means and where the boundary sits
topics.description: What integration means and where the boundary sits within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: The boundary rule, stated precisely
Unit tier: your server process, with OrderRepo, EmailSender, Clock substituted.

Integration tier: your server process plus a *real* Postgres, *real* Redis, a *real* HTTP server bound to an ephemeral port, and MSW intercepting the outbound third-party calls. Requests are made over TCP with Supertest/undici, not by calling handlers directly.
E2E tier: the browser talking to a real deployed-ish server, which talks to real infrastructure.
The "one real thing" heuristic

Isolation. Each test starts from a known database state and leaves no residue that affects another test. Options: transaction-per-test with rollback (fastest, 9.2.4), truncate-and-reseed per test (simple, order-independent, slower), or a fresh schema/database per worker (parallel-safe, needs a template database or container).

Realism of the code path. Do not import a handler and call it. Start the server, make an HTTP request. Every layer above the database must be the production layer: the real router, the real middleware chain, the real DI container.

Speed. A suite that takes 20 minutes will be skipped. Target 30-120 seconds for the whole integration tier by using an ephemeral in-process database, connection pooling, and parallelism across workers.
Where the boundary sits -- four judgement calls, with the reasoning

Do you use a real database or a fake repository? Real. An in-memory fake repo cannot catch a missing NOT NULL, an index, a transaction boundary, or a timestamptz timezone bug, and those are the bugs that reach production. The cost (startup time) is paid once with Testcontainers (9.2.5) or PGlite (an in-process WASM Postgres, which is not a fake -- it is the real engine).

Do you mock third-party APIs? Yes, at the *network* boundary with MSW (9.2.6), because a real third-party call in CI is slow, flaky, billable, and (for sign-up flows) ethically fraught. But mock at HTTP, not at your own adapter's method, so your adapter's serialisation is still under test.

Do you use the production DI container? Yes, with a *test* composition root that swaps only adapters you are deliberately substituting. If your test builds the object graph by hand, the test will not catch a missing binding in main.ts -- which is a real and common bug.

topics.title: Supertest and testing HTTP endpoints end to end
topics.description: Supertest and testing HTTP endpoints end to end within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Supertest
The full test surface, not just the happy path
Speed. Each supertest(app) call starts an ephemeral server per request. For large suites, create one server and reuse it (Supertest handles this internally when you pass the same app).
Header/cookie fidelity. Supertest uses a real http.ClientRequest, so cookies, Set-Cookie, and Authorization behave as in production -- a genuine advantage over inject.
Async leaks. If your app has a setInterval or an open DB pool, the test process will not exit. You must call h.close(). A suite that "hangs after tests pass" is the most common Supertest complaint.
No browser semantics. No cookies-with-SameSite enforcement, no CORS preflight unless you ask for OPTIONS, no service worker. Those are E2E or explicit-header tests.
One harness module, imported by every integration spec. Never build the app inside a test.

Use real auth (sign a real token with the test secret) rather than a bypass header like x-test-user; the bypass header is a permanent backdoor in production and is the single most dangerous thing in this list.
Assert on the error envelope for every 4xx/5xx, not just the status code. The error shape is a contract your clients depend on.
Add a --keep-db mode and print the failing request/response to make triage possible.
In CI, run the integration suite with maxWorkers tuned to the number of DB connections, not to the number of CPU cores, or you will exhaust the pool and generate fake flakes.
Forgetting await on the Supertest promise (Supertest is thenable, so this mostly works, but expect(app.get(...).expect(200)) does not).

topics.title: Database seeding, fixtures, and test isolation
topics.description: Database seeding, fixtures, and test isolation within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Seeding
Why transaction-per-test usually works and when it does not
your code under test commits inside the test (a prisma.$transaction nested call, a separate connection, a COMMIT in raw SQL) -- then the test's rollback cannot undo it;
your code uses two connections concurrently (a queue worker polling while the request runs) -- the worker's changes are not in your transaction;
you need to test READ COMMITTED vs SERIALIZABLE behaviour with two actors;
the code uses LISTEN/NOTIFY, advisory locks, or advisory-based coordination across connections.
Seeders: minimal, relational, and derived from production types
Isolation patterns for the cases transaction-per-test cannot cover
No data at all when the test creates what it needs inline (the best option; no shared fixture, no cross-test coupling).
Factory-per-test for one or two entities.
Seeding helpers for three or more tests needing the same graph (e.g. a user with a saved card and a past order).

Bulk seeding (createMany, generate_series in raw SQL) for pagination, performance, and load tests. Use raw SQL for >10 000 rows; createMany is still one statement per batch and is slow beyond a few thousand.

topics.title: Transaction-per-test and rollback-based cleanup
topics.description: Transaction-per-test and rollback-based cleanup within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Transaction-per-test

Postgres (and every serious relational DB) gives you a transaction with READ COMMITTED (or stronger) isolation. A row inserted inside your test's transaction is invisible to any *other* connection, and vanishes on ROLLBACK.
By handing your code a trx client instead of the global prisma client, every statement it issues participates in that transaction, so its writes are also rolled back.
No DELETE, no TRUNCATE, no re-seeding reference data, no sequence-reset logic. Cleanup cost is O(1) -- a network round trip for ROLLBACK.
Tests can run in parallel against the *same* database, because their writes are mutually invisible.
What you must do to make it work (the four rules)

The code under test must use the transactional client. Either pass a client explicitly (the best design), or set a per-request client on an AsyncLocalStorage-scoped context. A module-level new PrismaClient() singleton in production code makes this impossible -- which is itself an argument for dependency injection.
Nothing may commit. Any prisma.$transaction() nested inside your test's transaction becomes a *savepoint* (Prisma does this correctly), which is fine, but raw COMMIT or a second connection is not.
Nothing may use a second connection. Background workers, event consumers, and LISTEN/NOTIFY listeners all escape the transaction. Tests for those must use the truncate strategy.
Long transactions can hold locks. Keep tests under a few seconds; set a statement_timeout inside the test transaction so a runaway query fails fast rather than blocking other workers.
Implementation B, complete, with the HTTP layer wired in
Timeouts, locks, and safety rails

topics.title: Testcontainers: real dependencies without shared dev boxes
topics.description: Testcontainers: real dependencies without shared dev boxes within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Testcontainers
Container start. A container image is started with a specific configuration (image tag or digest, env, command, port bindings, mounted volumes, a tmpfs for speed).

Wait strategy. The container is not ready when docker run returns. Testcontainers uses a *wait strategy* -- waitForListeningPort(), wait.forLogMessage(), wait.forHealthCheck(), or a custom wait -- and blocks until the dependency is genuinely usable.
Connection details. getMappedPort(5432) and getHost() produce a connection URL. Because ports are dynamic, every test file must read the URL from the container, never hardcode 5432.
Reuse. withReuse() keeps the container alive between runs (a huge local speedup) and requires opt-in (testcontainers.reuse.enable=true in ~/.testcontainers.properties).
Teardown. Ryuk (the resource reaper container) monitors the JVM/Node process and kills orphans when it dies, so a crashed run does not leak containers.
The "system under test in a container" pattern

Requires a working Docker daemon. In restricted CI, in some corporate networks, and on machines without Docker, this is a hard blocker. Have a fallback: an env var pointing at a managed Postgres (TEST_DATABASE_URL), and a documented "no Docker? use this" path.
Startup cost. 1-5s per container, serialised. globalSetup amortises it across the whole run. Reuse eliminates it locally.
Resource use. Each container needs memory; 8 workers each starting a container will exhaust a laptop. Start once per process, not per file.

Cleanup is best-effort. A hard kill (CI runner OOM) can leak containers. Ryuk handles the common case; add a CI step docker ps -aq --filter "label=org.testcontainers=true" | xargs -r docker rm -f for safety.
Image drift. postgres:16 moves under you. Pin a minor (16.4) or a digest, and consider a nightly job against the newest minor to catch deprecations before your users do.

topics.description: MSW: mocking at the network boundary within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Mock Service Worker (MSW)

Request handlers (declarative, default). http.get('/api/user', () => HttpResponse.json({...})) registered on a setupServer instance. Used in tests and in node (Vitest/Jest). Handlers are matched in reverse registration order (last registered wins), with optional path params, wildcards, and predicates.

Storybook-style handlers (in-browser, for development). msw-storybook-addon lets you define handlers once and use them both as a mock backend for Storybook and as the test backend, guaranteeing that stories exercise the same contract as tests.
Handler design: base handlers plus per-test overrides
Cassettes / record-and-replay
Your outbound adapter's behaviour is now genuinely tested -- the big win. URL construction, headers, auth, serialisation, timeouts, retries, and error mapping all run for real.

It is a fake server, so the provider's real behaviour is still unknown. MSW proves you speak the protocol you *think* the provider speaks. Contract tests (9.2.7) and periodic sandbox runs close the remaining gap.

onUnhandledRequest: 'error' is a setting you should make and keep. It turns "my handler has the wrong URL" into an immediate, obvious failure instead of a mysterious 404 from the wrong place. In development/Storybook, use 'bypass'.

Service Worker mode has gotchas: it requires a secure context (localhost counts), it can serve stale handlers until unregistered, and in Playwright you must route MSW's worker script or disable SW. In Node, @mswjs/interceptors patches http/fetch/XHR, which does not intercept a raw net.Socket write.

Latency simulation with delay() is the fastest way to write a debounce/spinner test -- and also the fastest way to introduce a real-time flake if you forget it is real. Prefer advanceTimersByTimeAsync with fake timers, or keep the delay well under the test timeout.
Keep handlers in one module, imported by tests, Storybook, and the dev server. Single source of truth for the backend shape is the entire value.
Generate handlers from your OpenAPI/GraphQL schema where you can (msw-openapi-har or openapi-msw), so a schema change breaks the handler set rather than silently serving stale shapes.

keyConcepts: Runnable code -- the consumer side (Pact-JS / pact-js)
Runnable code -- the provider side (verification)
Provider state is where contracts rot
Matcher strictness is the design decision that matters most in CDC

You get decoupling and a real change-warning mechanism; you pay for it in ceremony: a broker, a state-setup endpoint, per-field matcher decisions, and a provider verification job. For two teams this is a clear win; for twenty services it is an operational platform you must staff.

Pacts are *tolerant* by default: unlisted fields are ignored and extra requests cause a failure only if you configure it. This is right for additive change and wrong for accidental behaviour change. Use allowUnexpectedRequests: false if you want strictness, accepting that it will flag benign additions.

Canary deployments solve the "which pact version do I verify?" problem: the provider verifies against the consumer version that will actually be deployed (or soon will be), which is what consumerVersionSelectors with deployedOrRelease gives you.

State setup is real work and a real maintenance burden. A state that takes 20 lines of seeding is a state nobody will add, and a missing state means a failed verification, which means teams learn to --skip verification, which kills the whole mechanism.
A generated mock cannot be the source of truth for the provider's own tests. Pact verifies the provider; it does not improve the provider's test suite.
Run provider verification in CI before deploy, and block the pipeline on failure. A green main branch that has not been verified against canary consumer pacts is a broken gate.
Tag consumer pacts: main (the current stable), prod (what is deployed), and feature branches. Then the provider can ask the broker "what am I about to break?"
Use the PactFlow (or PactSafe-style) CI integration so the Slack notification and the PR comment come for free.

topics.title: Service mocking without lying to yourself
topics.description: Service mocking without lying to yourself within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Anti-patterns, with the specific failure each causes
The four verification mechanisms that keep you honest
Contract-test the double. Write one suite that runs against both the fake and the real implementation.
Use recorded fixtures from the real system. For outbound third-party clients, record a real response once and assert the fake reproduces it.
Type the double as the real port and forbid divergence.

Assert the negative space. For every mock, assert the paths that the mock would *not* let you reach: timeouts, cancellation, malformed responses, partial responses, HTTP 429, HTTP 5xx, connection reset.
"Do not mock the thing you own to test the thing you own."

Mocks are fast and precise; reality is slow and messy. The cost of a mock is that it is a hypothesis. The cost of reality is a 3-second test, a container, and a schema you have to keep in sync. You pay the second cost exactly once per dependency, in the contract test, and then you get the first cost everywhere else.

A contract test is a real, ongoing cost that is easy to forget. It is, however, dramatically cheaper than the incident it prevents ("we assumed the provider returns 200 on a soft decline; it returns 202 with status: pending").

A mock-heavy suite is a knowledge transfer problem. The next engineer must reconstruct the real behaviour from the mocks. Where you can, prefer MSW so that the real adapter code is the thing being described.
Mocking your own pure function, so the logic is never tested.
A mock whose return value is narrower than reality, so your real serialisation/deserialisation path is never executed.

topics.title: Error simulation and testing failure paths
topics.description: Error simulation and testing failure paths within Integration Testing.
keyConcepts: Error simulation
Database failure simulation
Observability assertions -- the failure path you almost never test
Testing partial failure in a batch
The reliability-pattern tests you should always have
When to focus on failure paths

Failure tests are the highest-value and least-maintained tests in most suites. They tend to be written once during an incident and then rot as the code changes shape. Budget for rewriting them when you refactor the client.
Simulating real socket-level failures requires real servers, which is slower and less portable than MSW. Use MSW for protocol-level failures and a real net.Server for transport-level ones.

Injecting timeouts via delay('infinite') in MSW is real time. A 1500ms timeout test takes 1.5s. With 20 such tests that is 30 seconds. Consider delay(10) with a client timeout of 5ms for speed, accepting that it tests the timeout logic rather than the exact duration, and keep one test with realistic numbers.
Killing a database backend is genuinely disruptive -- it will fail *other* tests running in parallel. Only do it in a dedicated, serialised suite.
Testing only the 4xx paths, because they are easy to trigger with a mock, and never the 5xx/timeout/reset paths.
Asserting only the status code on the error path, not the error code, the log, and the metric.

topics.title: Cypress
topics.description: Cypress within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: Cypress
The superpowers

Time travel. Every test command is recorded with a snapshot of the DOM, the JavaScript state, network activity, and console output at that moment. When a test fails, you can hover backwards and inspect the application exactly as it was.
Debuggability by construction. cy.pause() opens a real debugger at that point in the test, and failures open the DevTools automatically.
Deterministic command queue. Commands are enqueued and executed in order, with retries on assertions (should('be.visible') retries for 4s by default), so you do not write waits.
The constraint
It cannot run multiple tabs natively.
It cannot visit two superdomains in one test (cross-origin navigation is restricted; cy.visit to a different origin is not supported in the same test).
It is not a real WebDriver, so testing native browser features (the file picker, some OS dialogs, WebAuthn, real downloads in some modes) is harder.
It requires a proxy in front of your app, which is a real deployment-shape difference (and occasionally a real source of CORS/cookie bugs that do not exist in production).

keyConcepts: Playwright
Auto-waiting, and the two things that defeat it
Web-first assertions
Browser contexts: the isolation unit
The config that makes a suite fast and useful
Network control, which is the escape hatch you must have
Tracing and debugging

WebKit on Linux is not Safari. It is close (same engine lineage) but not identical: font rendering, media codecs, and some platform APIs differ. Visual baselines must be generated per platform, and you should keep one real-Mac or BrowserStack job for Safari if Safari matters.

fullyParallel: true inside a file is a step change for suite size, and it *forces* per-test data isolation. Teams that enable it must adopt API-based setup and namespaced cleanup; otherwise they trade slowness for flake.
Retry = 1 is a policy, not a setting. A suite with 3% flake and retries: 2 will be green and worthless. Track the flake rate (flaky-tests reporter) and treat it as a P1.

Auto-waiting hides real UX problems in the sense that it waits for *stability*; a spinner that never resolves simply times out. That is a feature. But auto-waiting cannot wait for a condition your app never expresses in the DOM, so a test that needs waitForFunction is telling you the app lacks an observable state.
Trace files are large (5-30MB). Budget artifact storage, upload on failure only, and set a retention policy.

topics.title: Selenium
topics.description: Selenium within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: Selenium
Why you still need to know it (2026)
It is the only option for some environments: real Safari on real macOS via safaridriver (managed by Apple), legacy devices, and some enterprise grids.
It is the substrate of Appium, which drives native and hybrid mobile apps with the same WebDriver model. Any mobile native-testing strategy you meet will use it.
It is the interop reference for any automation tool: WebDriver is the standard the other tools are measured against.
Many organisations have an existing Selenium suite or grid, and migrating is a project, not a decision.
Understanding the protocol makes you understand what the modern tools abstract away (the session, the element lookup, the shadow root, the action sequence, the document readiness).
The four hard parts of Selenium, and how the modern tools solve them

Waiting. WebDriver is unopinionated: an element may be located but not yet clickable, and click() throws ElementNotInteractableException. The answer is driver.wait(until.elementIsVisible(...)) or explicit ExpectedConditions. Every Selenium suite is 30% waiting code. Playwright and Cypress build retrying locators into the API, so this code does not exist.

Driver/browsers version matching. Historically the biggest tax in Selenium. Selenium Manager (4.6+) bundles a binary that resolves and caches the right driver for the installed browser. This single change removed a whole category of support tickets.

Grid and distribution. Selenium Grid 4 provides a hub and node architecture, W3C-compliant, with Docker/Kubernetes deployment and session routing policies (strict, dynamic, fixed). It is still the answer for "we must run on 40 real devices/OS versions in one place".
No first-class tracing. You build artifact capture yourself (screenshots, getPageSource, network logs via BiDi). Modern tools do this for you.

Nondeterminism. Animations, transitions, carousels, clocks, random data, cursor position, and scrollbars produce different pixels on every run.
Font rendering differences between OSes and even between machines with different font versions.
Sub-pixel and anti-aliasing noise from fractional layout.
Dynamic content (dates, names, "3 minutes ago", randomised ids).
Where visual baselines live, and how they are reviewed
Keep the baseline count low. 20-40 screenshots per platform for critical screens; not every page. Visual coverage of stable, high-value screens only.
Group shots into few files. One screenshot per "state" (empty, loading, error, populated, mobile, desktop) rather than one per component.
Freeze a platform for baselines. Generate them in the same container image you compare in, so fonts and rendering are identical. In CI, use the official Playwright Docker image.
Threshold is not a licence. A 5% diff ratio on a text-heavy page will accept a completely different paragraph. Prefer masking text to loosening thresholds.

```yaml
          TEST_REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4

    needs: [verify]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
```

```bash
# It does NOT balance by duration. A suite where one spec file takes 6 minutes
# and 40 files take 5 seconds each will have one shard that takes 6 minutes.

  const r = require('./run.json');

  const byFile = {};

    bins.sort((a,b) => a.d-b.d)[0].files.add(f); bins[0].d += ds.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
```

topics.title: Flaky test causes and fixes
topics.description: Flaky test causes and fixes within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: The taxonomy. Every flaky test fits one of these eleven classes
1. Race condition / missing await
*Symptoms:* "expected undefined", intermittent 0/1 counts, tests that pass in isolation and fail in a suite.

*Causes:* a promise not awaited; setTimeout instead of awaiting an event; a test that finishes before an async effect completes; fireEvent instead of userEvent; an assertion immediately after an action.
*Fixes:* await the promise the function returns; assert with findBy*/waitFor; use userEvent; never assert in the same tick as an action; expect.assertions(n).
*Detection:* run the file 1000 times (--repeat-each 1000) and look at the failure distribution; enable --sequence.shuffle.
2. Shared state / test interdependence
*Symptoms:* passes alone, fails in the suite; order-dependent; "works on a clean checkout".

*Causes:* a module-level mutable object; a shared file, port, or database; a shared storageState; a beforeAll that seeds without cleanup; a global cache in the app under test; a singleton Prisma/HTTP client with per-test config.

*Fixes:* one fresh state per test (beforeEach); namespaced data; per-worker databases; fullyParallel (which forces the issue); vi.resetModules(); clearAllMocks in afterEach; never mutate module-scope fixtures.
*Detection:* --sequence.shuffle; run with --maxWorkers=1 (if it passes serial, it is shared state).
3. Real time and timers

topics.title: Page object model
topics.description: Page object model within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: The POM that hides the test -- the failure mode, named
The page object returns data and the test asserts everything. Then the page object is a "getter bag" and the assertions are in the test; you have the worst of both.
The page object contains business logic. await cart.applyCouponIfOrderOver(50) now duplicates a pricing rule that a unit test owns, and it will drift.
The page object hides failures. A method that internally retries, catches, and falls back will make a broken app look like a passing test.
The page object is a one-line wrapper. get addButton() { return this.page.locator('#add') } adds indirection and no value.

Selectors are stored as fields at construction time. private readonly qty = page.locator('#qty') binds the locator before navigation; in Playwright a locator is lazy so this is usually fine, but with page.$ (a promise) it captures the wrong element. Always store the Page, not resolved elements.

One page object per screen means N objects per test. The combinatorial cost is what pushes teams to abandon the pattern -- and then the selectors leak back into the tests, and every copy change breaks 40 tests.
The decision rule, and what to do instead
POM pros: one place to change when the UI changes; readable tests; reusable flows; a natural home for waits and for i18n; keeps test files focused on intent.

POM cons: indirection makes failures harder to localise (a stack trace points into the page object, not the test); over-abstraction makes tests read like a DSL nobody but the author can use; and a page object per screen multiplies the files you must maintain.

Capability objects beat page objects on intent-readability and navigation-resilience, at the cost of being less "reusable" for flows that only one test uses. Given that E2E suites should be small and intent-focused, this is the right trade.

Never put assertions in a page object that are about the *test's* data (e.g. "this order is in the database"); keep those in the test. Assertions about the *screen's* state belong with the screen's capability.

topics.title: Test pyramid vs trophy
topics.description: Test pyramid vs trophy within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: The two shapes, side by side
Which shape to use, and the reasoning behind the choice
The economics, quantified

E2E's value per engineering hour is the lowest and its CI/triage cost is the highest. 28 tests costing 3 hours a week and 45 minutes of triage per failure. That is the argument for *fewer, better* E2E tests, not for more.

Component tests have the best ratio in a front-end project, which is precisely the trophy's argument: they catch real wiring bugs (providers, queries, routing, event handling) at a third of the E2E cost and a fiftieth of the triage cost.
The tier that is cheap and ungated is worth keeping ungated (perf, visual): running them on every PR costs more than it catches.
Triage time, not runtime, is the dominant E2E cost. 45 minutes per failure is the real number, and it is driven by the quality of your traces and failure messages, not by the test's speed.
It corresponds to a stated behaviour or risk, not to a line of code. (If you cannot name the behaviour, you are writing a change-detector.)
It fails when the behaviour breaks. Verify this by mutating the implementation (9.4.4). If it does not fail, the test is not paying.
It is deterministic and fast enough to run often. A 3-minute integration test run 40 times a week is fine; a 3-minute test run once is decoration.
Its maintenance cost is bounded. If it will need rewriting on every refactor, the tier is wrong (implementation-detail test) or the seam is wrong.
The behaviour it covers is more likely to change than to be deleted, or it is so critical that even a stable behaviour must stay verified (money, permissions, safety).

Prove the whole thing works together, once. A smoke test that the deployed artefact boots, authenticates, and completes the primary conversion. This is the "is the release actually shippable" gate.

Verify the boundaries that only exist in the browser and in production configuration. Verify business rules. Discount maths belongs in a unit/property test where it runs 5000 times in 40ms. In E2E you can check *one* example.
Cover UI layout exhaustively. That is component testing plus visual regression.
Be a substitute for a fast feedback loop. A developer who waits 6 minutes to learn their typo broke the build has been taught to batch work, and batching work is how defects enter.

Auto-waiting, and the two things that defeat it
Web-first assertions

The config that makes a suite fast and useful
Network control, which is the escape hatch you must have

WebKit on Linux is not Safari. It is close (same engine lineage) but not identical: font rendering, media codecs, and some platform APIs differ. Visual baselines must be generated per platform, and you should keep one real-Mac or BrowserStack job for Safari if Safari matters.

topics.title: Cypress: its model and where it differs
topics.description: Cypress: its model and where it differs within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: Cypress
The superpowers

Time travel. Every test command is recorded with a snapshot of the DOM, the JavaScript state, network activity, and console output at that moment. When a test fails, you can hover backwards and inspect the application exactly as it was.
Debuggability by construction. cy.pause() opens a real debugger at that point in the test, and failures open the DevTools automatically.
Deterministic command queue. Commands are enqueued and executed in order, with retries on assertions (should('be.visible') retries for 4s by default), so you do not write waits.
The constraint
It cannot run multiple tabs natively.
It cannot visit two superdomains in one test (cross-origin navigation is restricted; cy.visit to a different origin is not supported in the same test).
It is not a real WebDriver, so testing native browser features (the file picker, some OS dialogs, WebAuthn, real downloads in some modes) is harder.
It requires a proxy in front of your app, which is a real deployment-shape difference (and occasionally a real source of CORS/cookie bugs that do not exist in production).

topics.description: Selenium and the WebDriver protocol, for awareness within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: Selenium
Why you still need to know it (2026)
It is the only option for some environments: real Safari on real macOS via safaridriver (managed by Apple), legacy devices, and some enterprise grids.
It is the substrate of Appium, which drives native and hybrid mobile apps with the same WebDriver model. Any mobile native-testing strategy you meet will use it.
It is the interop reference for any automation tool: WebDriver is the standard the other tools are measured against.
Many organisations have an existing Selenium suite or grid, and migrating is a project, not a decision.
Understanding the protocol makes you understand what the modern tools abstract away (the session, the element lookup, the shadow root, the action sequence, the document readiness).
The four hard parts of Selenium, and how the modern tools solve them

Waiting. WebDriver is unopinionated: an element may be located but not yet clickable, and click() throws ElementNotInteractableException. The answer is driver.wait(until.elementIsVisible(...)) or explicit ExpectedConditions. Every Selenium suite is 30% waiting code. Playwright and Cypress build retrying locators into the API, so this code does not exist.

Driver/browsers version matching. Historically the biggest tax in Selenium. Selenium Manager (4.6+) bundles a binary that resolves and caches the right driver for the installed browser. This single change removed a whole category of support tickets.

Grid and distribution. Selenium Grid 4 provides a hub and node architecture, W3C-compliant, with Docker/Kubernetes deployment and session routing policies (strict, dynamic, fixed). It is still the answer for "we must run on 40 real devices/OS versions in one place".
No first-class tracing. You build artifact capture yourself (screenshots, getPageSource, network logs via BiDi). Modern tools do this for you.

Nondeterminism. Animations, transitions, carousels, clocks, random data, cursor position, and scrollbars produce different pixels on every run.
Font rendering differences between OSes and even between machines with different font versions.
Sub-pixel and anti-aliasing noise from fractional layout.

Where visual baselines live, and how they are reviewed

keyConcepts: Network condition testing
The behaviours worth testing (the canonical list)
When to test network conditions

Throttling makes tests slow -- a 3G test can take 30s. Keep it to one or two tests per critical journey, and use page.route delays (portable) rather than CDP throughput emulation (accurate but Chromium-only and slower).

CDP network emulation is Chromium-only, so a throttling test in the WebKit/Firefox projects will silently do nothing if you write it with newCDPSession. Guard it with test.skip(browserName !== 'chromium') or use route-based delays.

Service workers complicate everything. A service worker may serve a cached response and never hit the network, so your throttle test measures nothing. Test service-worker behaviour explicitly (a dedicated context with serviceWorkers: 'block', and another with them enabled).
Realistic offline testing requires a real offline story. If the app has no offline capability, "offline" is just "an error page", and that is a product finding, not a test.
Randomised fault injection produces flaky tests. Make faults deterministic (specific paths, specific counts, specific order) so a failure is reproducible.
setOffline on the context but the app uses a service worker that serves from cache, so nothing changes.
Testing throttling in the WebKit project with a CDP-only call.
Asserting a fixed time (expect(elapsed).toBeGreaterThan(3000)), which is a load test not an E2E test.
Not testing the *reconnect* path, which is where duplicate writes and data loss live.

```yaml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true                 # never waste CI on a superseded commit

jobs:
  # ── Stage 1: the fast gate. 20 seconds, hard required. Nobody waits for this.
  verify:
    name: Lint, types, unit, property
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint
      - run: pnpm typecheck                     # tsc --noEmit, separate from tests on purpose
      - run: pnpm test:unit -- --coverage
      - run: pnpm test:property
      - run: pnpm test:mutation --changed        # Stryker on changed files only
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: coverage, path: coverage/ }

  # ── Stage 2: integration. Parallel with stage 1 where the dependency graph allows.
  integration:
    name: Integration (Postgres, Redis)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16.4-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: test
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
          POSTGRES_DB: app_test
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U test -d app_test"
          --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10
      redis:
        image: redis:7.4-alpine
        ports: ['6379:6379']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping" --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm test:integration
        env:
          TEST_DATABASE_URL: postgres://test:test@localhost:5432/app_test
          TEST_REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with: { name: integration-diagnostics, path: test-artifacts/ }

  # ── Stage 3: build once, reuse for E2E and preview deploy.
  build:
    needs: [verify]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      image: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm build
      - id: meta
        run: echo "image=ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  # ── Stage 4: E2E against a preview environment built from the PR artefact.
  e2e:
    needs: [build]
    if: contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'e2e') || github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false                        # keep siblings running: their traces are the evidence
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: pnpm exec playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
        env:
          E2E_BASE_URL: ${{ needs.deploy-preview.outputs.url }}
          RUN_ID: ${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with: { name: trace-${{ matrix.shard }}, path: e2e/.artifacts }

  # ── Stage 5: what blocks the merge.
  required:
    needs: [verify, integration, e2e]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: |
          echo "verify=${{ needs.verify.result }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "integration=${{ needs.integration.result }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "e2e=${{ needs.e2e.result }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: |
          test "${{ needs.verify.result }}" = "success"
          test "${{ needs.integration.result }}" = "success"
          if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" = "push" ]; then
            test "${{ needs.e2e.result }}" = "success"
          else
            echo "::notice::E2E is advisory on PRs; required on main."
          fi

  # ── Stage 6: nightly. The expensive matrix that must not gate every PR.
  nightly:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - run: pnpm exec playwright test --project=chromium --project=firefox --project=webkit --project=mobile-chrome
      - run: pnpm test:mutation
      - run: pnpm audit --audit-level=high
```

```bash
# Playwright shards by *file*, and --shard=n/total splits the file list.
# It does NOT balance by duration. A suite where one spec file takes 6 minutes
# and 40 files take 5 seconds each will have one shard that takes 6 minutes.
#
# Measure and rebalance:
npx playwright test --list                      # list all tests
npx playwright test --reporter=json > run.json   # per-test durations from the last run
node -e "                                        # greedy bin-packing by duration
  const r = require('./run.json');
  const shards = 4, bins = Array.from({length: shards}, () => ({d:0, files:new Set()}));
  const byFile = {};
  for (const s of r.suites.flatMap(s => s.specs)) {
    const f = s.file; (byFile[f] ||= []).push(s.tests[0]?.results?.[0]?.duration ?? 0);
  }
  for (const [f, ds] of Object.entries(byFile).sort((a,b) => b[1][0]-a[1][0])) {
    bins.sort((a,b) => a.d-b.d)[0].files.add(f); bins[0].d += ds.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
  }
  console.log(bins.map((b,i) => ({shard: i+1, files: b.files.size, seconds: Math.round(b.d/1000)})));
```
```yaml
"
```

topics.title: Flaky test causes and fixes: the complete catalogue
topics.description: Flaky test causes and fixes: the complete catalogue within End to End Testing.
keyConcepts: The taxonomy. Every flaky test fits one of these eleven classes
1. Race condition / missing await
*Symptoms:* "expected undefined", intermittent 0/1 counts, tests that pass in isolation and fail in a suite.

*Causes:* a promise not awaited; setTimeout instead of awaiting an event; a test that finishes before an async effect completes; fireEvent instead of userEvent; an assertion immediately after an action.
*Fixes:* await the promise the function returns; assert with findBy*/waitFor; use userEvent; never assert in the same tick as an action; expect.assertions(n).
*Detection:* run the file 1000 times (--repeat-each 1000) and look at the failure distribution; enable --sequence.shuffle.
2. Shared state / test interdependence
*Symptoms:* passes alone, fails in the suite; order-dependent; "works on a clean checkout".

*Causes:* a module-level mutable object; a shared file, port, or database; a shared storageState; a beforeAll that seeds without cleanup; a global cache in the app under test; a singleton Prisma/HTTP client with per-test config.

*Fixes:* one fresh state per test (beforeEach); namespaced data; per-worker databases; fullyParallel (which forces the issue); vi.resetModules(); clearAllMocks in afterEach; never mutate module-scope fixtures.
*Detection:* --sequence.shuffle; run with --maxWorkers=1 (if it passes serial, it is shared state).
3. Real time and timers

topics.title: Performance and load testing (k6, JMeter)
topics.description: Performance and load testing (k6, JMeter) within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: Performance testing
Runnable code -- a production-shaped k6 scenario for a checkout API
Threshold files and environment-driven configuration

Load tests measure the system you point them at, including the test environment's noise. A 2-core CI runner cannot generate meaningful load for a 32-core service; you will measure k6's own CPU. Check http_req_blocked and vus in the result, and generate from a machine at least as powerful as the target's load generator needs.
k6 is not a browser. It does not execute JavaScript, so it tests your API, not your frontend. For front-end performance, use Lighthouse/CrUX/web-vitals RUM data and Playwright for a synthetic check.

Thresholds are SLOs, not aspirations. A threshold you set to today's number guarantees the test never fails and therefore never helps. Set it to the number your users agreed to, and let it fail when you regress.

Load tests are not idempotent under mutation. A load test that creates 300 000 orders needs cleanup and a database big enough to hold them, or it measures the vacuum, not your service. Prefer a load-test mode that uses a read-heavy mix with a small write fraction, or a shadow/read replica, or reset the environment afterwards.
A load test that only does GETs will never find the write-concurrency bug. Include a write phase, and include a burst phase.
The p99 is where the pain is and where the tests are least stable. Gate on p95 in every-PR runs and p99 in nightly runs.
Run a nightly performance regression run against staging, and gate p95 and the error rate. Publish the result as a trend, not a pass/fail, so a gradual drift is visible.

Run a stress test on a schedule to find the breaking point and, more importantly, *how it fails*: does it degrade gracefully (errors, then recovery) or collapse (connection refused, cascading timeouts)? That answer is a resilience finding, not a performance finding.
Run a soak test (4-8 hours at 70% of peak) before any release that changes infrastructure, connection pooling, or anything that might leak. It catches the leaks that a 5-minute test cannot.
