topics.title: Accessibility testing
topics.description: Accessibility testing within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: Accessibility (a11y)

Automated scanning (axe-core, Lighthouse, Pa11y, eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y): catches roughly 20-40% of issues -- missing labels, contrast, missing alt, invalid ARIA, heading order, duplicate ids, focus order in simple cases.

Manual expert testing (keyboard, screen reader, zoom, forced colors, motion): catches the rest -- the ones a machine cannot judge (alt text *quality*, focus *visibility*, reading order *sense*, error message *clarity*, timeout sufficiency).
User testing with disabled people: catches what neither of the first two can -- whether the experience is actually usable and non-embarrassing.
The legal and commercial frame you need to know for interviews

Keyboard only. Unplug the mouse. Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, arrow keys. Every interactive element reachable, in a sensible order, with a visible focus indicator at every stop. No keyboard traps. Skip links work.

Screen reader (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, Orca on Linux). Learn the basics of one properly. Test: every image's alt text is *meaningful* (not "image1.jpg"); every form field has a label; errors are announced and associated; dynamic content is announced via a live region; the page has one h1 and a sane heading structure; tables have headers; the document language is set; landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) exist.
Zoom and reflow. 200% browser zoom, and 400% on a 1280px viewport (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow). No horizontal scrolling, no clipped content, no overlapping text.

Colour and contrast. Text contrast >= 4.5:1 (normal) and 3:1 (large, >= 24px or 19px bold). Non-text contrast >= 3:1 for UI components and focus indicators. Never colour alone to convey meaning. Check with a simulator for deuteranopia/protanopia/tritanopia and for achromatopsia.
Forced colours / high contrast mode (Windows High Contrast, prefers-contrast: more). Your custom colours often disappear.
Reduced motion. prefers-reduced-motion: reduce honoured: no parallax, no auto-playing carousels, no large transitions. prefers-reduced-transparency, prefers-contrast, forced-colors.
Text spacing (WCAG 1.4.12): with the bookmarklet applying 1.5x line-height, 1.5x letter-spacing, 4px word-spacing, 1.2x paragraph-spacing, nothing clips.
commonMistakes: an accessibility statement that claims conformance with a level you have not audited; automated checks run only pre-release; no issue tracking or SLA for a11y bugs; and treating WCAG as a checklist rather than as an outcome measured with disabled users.

topics.title: Security testing
topics.description: Security testing within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: Application security testing
The policy layer, which is where tools become a program
Pre-commit secret scanning, so secrets never reach the repository
SAST: always, on every commit, diff-aware so it is fast. Use a tuned ruleset (your framework's rules plus p/secrets and p/security-audit), not the entire Semgrep registry.
SCA: always, on the lockfile, with a policy that distinguishes direct from transitive and high from critical, and an SLA (e.g. critical within 48h).
Secret scanning: always, pre-commit and full history, plus platform-level (GitHub secret scanning / push protection) so leaks are blocked at the source.

DAST: nightly against staging. The passive/baseline scan is safe against a live environment and should also run after each deploy as a smoke check. The active/full scan only against an isolated, disposable environment.
Container/IaC scanning: on every image build and every IaC change.
False positives are the primary failure mode of every one of these tools. Without a baselined, ratcheting policy, the tools get muted. With one, they are effective. Budget for the policy work.

SAST cannot see authorisation logic. Its highest-value custom rules are the ones *you* write: "every route has the auth middleware", "no raw SQL with interpolation", "no PII in logs", "no process.env in client bundles". A generic ruleset will never find your business-logic authz holes; only review and the tests in 9.2.8 will.

DAST finds runtime issues SAST cannot (real injection through a real path, header misconfiguration, CORS, cookie flags) but has low coverage of authenticated and multi-step flows. Authenticated DAST needs a recorded authentication script, and that is fragile. DAST's best use is headers, cookies, TLS, CORS, and information disclosure.
SCA alert volume is enormous and mostly transitive. A policy of "critical/high in direct dependencies blocks; transitive is tracked weekly" is the only version of this that gets acted on.

# .github/workflows/security.yml
name: Security
on:
  pull_request:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  schedule: [{ cron: '17 3 * * *' }]        # nightly: the full set, including DAST

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write                     # for SARIF upload / code scanning

jobs:
  # ── 1. SAST: fast, every PR, diff-aware.
  sast:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }             # full history for some tools
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Semgrep (rules: p/default, p/security-audit, p/typescript, p/secrets)
        uses: returntocorp/semgrep-action@v1
        with:
          config: p/default
          generateSarif: true
        env: { SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN }} }
      - name: ESLint security rules (free, zero-config, catches the obvious)
        run: pnpm lint:security
      - name: CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with:
          languages: typescript,javascript
          queries: security-extended
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3

  # ── 2. SCA: every commit, and a hard policy on the diff.
  sca:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: OSV-Scanner (better advisory coverage than npm audit)
        run: |
          curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/osv-scanner/main/install.sh | sh
          osv-scanner scan source -r . --format json --output osv.json || true
          node scripts/osv-policy.mjs osv.json     # fail only on high/critical in *direct* deps
      - name: Licence check
        run: pnpm licenses list --json | npx license-checker --onlyAllow 'MIT;Apache-2.0;BSD-3-Clause;ISC;BSD-2-Clause' --production

  # ── 3. Secret scanning: pre-commit AND full history.
  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - name: Gitleaks (current tree + full history)
        run: |
          docker run -v "$PWD:/repo" zricethezav/gitleaks:latest detect \
            --source=/repo --report-format=sarif --report-path=gitleaks.sarif --redact
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()
        with: { sarif_file: gitleaks.sarif }

  # ── 4. Container + IaC scanning on every build.
  image-and-iac:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t $IMAGE:$SHA .
      - run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 --ignore-unfixed $IMAGE:$SHA
      - run: trivy fs --scanners misconfig,secret --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .

  # ── 5. DAST: nightly, against a staging deploy. Open-source and free.
  dast:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    needs: [deploy-staging]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Start ZAP baseline scan (passive: safe against a live app)
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/zap/wrk" -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable \
            zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.test \
              -c zap-baseline.conf -r zap-report.html -J zap-report.json -I || true
      - name: Start ZAP full scan (active: attacks; run against an isolated environment only)
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/zap/wrk" -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable \
            zap-full-scan.py -t https://staging.example.test -r zap-full.html || true
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: zap-report, path: zap-*.html }

  - id: no-raw-sql-interpolation
    patterns:
      - pattern-either:
          - pattern: $DB.query(`...${...}...`)
          - pattern: $DB.raw(`...${...}...`)

  - id: no-authorization-without-middleware

```js
// scripts/security-policy.mjs
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'

const SARIF = JSON.parse(readFileSync(process.argv[2], 'utf8'))
const findings = SARIF.runs.flatMap((r) =>
  r.results.map((res) => ({
    rule: res.ruleId,
    severity: res.level,
    file: res.locations?.[0]?.physicalLocation?.artifactLocation?.uri,
    line: res.locations?.[0]?.physicalLocation?.region?.startLine,
  })),
)

// 1. Fail on anything CRITICAL/HIGH unless it is baselined.
const baseline = new Set(JSON.parse(readFileSync('.security-baseline.json', 'utf8')).accepted)  // [{rule, file, line?}]
const NEW = findings.filter(
  (f) => ['critical', 'error', 'high'].includes(f.severity) &&
         !baseline.some((b) => b.rule === f.rule && b.file === f.file),
)

console.log(`scanned: ${findings.length} findings; new high/critical: ${NEW.length}; baselined: ${baseline.size}`)
if (process.argv.includes('--max-new') && NEW.length > Number(process.env.MAX_NEW_FINDINGS ?? 0)) {
  for (const f of NEW) console.error(`  ${f.severity} ${f.rule} ${f.file}:${f.line}`)
  process.exit(1)
}

// 2. Fail if the baseline has shrunk: a fixed finding must have its entry removed.
if (process.argv.includes('--ratchet')) {
  const stillPresent = new Set(findings.map((f) => `${f.rule}|${f.file}`))
  const stale = [...baseline].filter((b) => !stillPresent.has(`${b.rule}|${b.file}`))
  if (stale.length > 0) {
    console.error(`::error::${stale.length} baseline entries no longer match a finding. Remove them from .security-baseline.json.`)
    process.exit(1)
  }
}
```

keyConcepts: Code review
Review the description and the tests first, then the diff. If the tests do not demonstrate the requirement, the implementation is not reviewable yet. Most "bad reviews" are reviews of unclear intent.
Under 400 lines. Above that, the review is a skim. Split the PR. This is the single most effective rule in code review, and the one teams resist most.
One concern per PR. Refactor and behaviour change in the same commit is unreviewable: the reviewer cannot tell which lines are meant to change behaviour, so they either approve both or neither.
Review within hours, not days. Stale context makes a review a re-read. Time-box: first response within 4 working hours.
Distinguish the three comment classes explicitly, because conflating them is why reviews feel hostile:

Linting (ESLint + plugins): style, correctness patterns, React hooks rules, import hygiene, and framework-specific correctness (a11y, security, promise misuse, testing-library rules).
Type checking (TypeScript): the single highest-value static analysis you can adopt, because it verifies contracts across module boundaries that no test asserts.

topics.title: Performance and load testing with k6
topics.description: Performance and load testing with k6 within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: Performance testing
Runnable code -- a production-shaped k6 scenario for a checkout API
Threshold files and environment-driven configuration

Load tests measure the system you point them at, including the test environment's noise. A 2-core CI runner cannot generate meaningful load for a 32-core service; you will measure k6's own CPU. Check http_req_blocked and vus in the result, and generate from a machine at least as powerful as the target's load generator needs.
k6 is not a browser. It does not execute JavaScript, so it tests your API, not your frontend. For front-end performance, use Lighthouse/CrUX/web-vitals RUM data and Playwright for a synthetic check.

Thresholds are SLOs, not aspirations. A threshold you set to today's number guarantees the test never fails and therefore never helps. Set it to the number your users agreed to, and let it fail when you regress.

Load tests are not idempotent under mutation. A load test that creates 300 000 orders needs cleanup and a database big enough to hold them, or it measures the vacuum, not your service. Prefer a load-test mode that uses a read-heavy mix with a small write fraction, or a shadow/read replica, or reset the environment afterwards.
A load test that only does GETs will never find the write-concurrency bug. Include a write phase, and include a burst phase.
The p99 is where the pain is and where the tests are least stable. Gate on p95 in every-PR runs and p99 in nightly runs.
Run a nightly performance regression run against staging, and gate p95 and the error rate. Publish the result as a trend, not a pass/fail, so a gradual drift is visible.

Run a stress test on a schedule to find the breaking point and, more importantly, *how it fails*: does it degrade gracefully (errors, then recovery) or collapse (connection refused, cascading timeouts)? That answer is a resilience finding, not a performance finding.
Run a soak test (4-8 hours at 70% of peak) before any release that changes infrastructure, connection pooling, or anything that might leak. It catches the leaks that a 5-minute test cannot.

topics.title: Accessibility testing: automated, manual, and assistive-technology testing
topics.description: Accessibility testing: automated, manual, and assistive-technology testing within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: Accessibility (a11y)

Automated scanning (axe-core, Lighthouse, Pa11y, eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y): catches roughly 20-40% of issues -- missing labels, contrast, missing alt, invalid ARIA, heading order, duplicate ids, focus order in simple cases.

Manual expert testing (keyboard, screen reader, zoom, forced colors, motion): catches the rest -- the ones a machine cannot judge (alt text *quality*, focus *visibility*, reading order *sense*, error message *clarity*, timeout sufficiency).
User testing with disabled people: catches what neither of the first two can -- whether the experience is actually usable and non-embarrassing.
The legal and commercial frame you need to know for interviews

Keyboard only. Unplug the mouse. Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, arrow keys. Every interactive element reachable, in a sensible order, with a visible focus indicator at every stop. No keyboard traps. Skip links work.

Screen reader (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, Orca on Linux). Learn the basics of one properly. Test: every image's alt text is *meaningful* (not "image1.jpg"); every form field has a label; errors are announced and associated; dynamic content is announced via a live region; the page has one h1 and a sane heading structure; tables have headers; the document language is set; landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) exist.
Zoom and reflow. 200% browser zoom, and 400% on a 1280px viewport (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow). No horizontal scrolling, no clipped content, no overlapping text.

Colour and contrast. Text contrast >= 4.5:1 (normal) and 3:1 (large, >= 24px or 19px bold). Non-text contrast >= 3:1 for UI components and focus indicators. Never colour alone to convey meaning. Check with a simulator for deuteranopia/protanopia/tritanopia and for achromatopsia.
Forced colours / high contrast mode (Windows High Contrast, prefers-contrast: more). Your custom colours often disappear.
Reduced motion. prefers-reduced-motion: reduce honoured: no parallax, no auto-playing carousels, no large transitions. prefers-reduced-transparency, prefers-contrast, forced-colors.
Text spacing (WCAG 1.4.12): with the bookmarklet applying 1.5x line-height, 1.5x letter-spacing, 4px word-spacing, 1.2x paragraph-spacing, nothing clips.
commonMistakes: an accessibility statement that claims conformance with a level you have not audited; automated checks run only pre-release; no issue tracking or SLA for a11y bugs; and treating WCAG as a checklist rather than as an outcome measured with disabled users.

topics.description: Security testing: SAST, DAST, SCA, and secret scanning in the pipeline within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: Application security testing
The policy layer, which is where tools become a program
Pre-commit secret scanning, so secrets never reach the repository
SAST: always, on every commit, diff-aware so it is fast. Use a tuned ruleset (your framework's rules plus p/secrets and p/security-audit), not the entire Semgrep registry.
SCA: always, on the lockfile, with a policy that distinguishes direct from transitive and high from critical, and an SLA (e.g. critical within 48h).
Secret scanning: always, pre-commit and full history, plus platform-level (GitHub secret scanning / push protection) so leaks are blocked at the source.

DAST: nightly against staging. The passive/baseline scan is safe against a live environment and should also run after each deploy as a smoke check. The active/full scan only against an isolated, disposable environment.
Container/IaC scanning: on every image build and every IaC change.
False positives are the primary failure mode of every one of these tools. Without a baselined, ratcheting policy, the tools get muted. With one, they are effective. Budget for the policy work.

SAST cannot see authorisation logic. Its highest-value custom rules are the ones *you* write: "every route has the auth middleware", "no raw SQL with interpolation", "no PII in logs", "no process.env in client bundles". A generic ruleset will never find your business-logic authz holes; only review and the tests in 9.2.8 will.

DAST finds runtime issues SAST cannot (real injection through a real path, header misconfiguration, CORS, cookie flags) but has low coverage of authenticated and multi-step flows. Authenticated DAST needs a recorded authentication script, and that is fragile. DAST's best use is headers, cookies, TLS, CORS, and information disclosure.
SCA alert volume is enormous and mostly transitive. A policy of "critical/high in direct dependencies blocks; transitive is tracked weekly" is the only version of this that gets acted on.

on:
  pull_request:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  schedule: [{ cron: '17 3 * * *' }]        # nightly: the full set, including DAST

jobs:

  sast:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }             # full history for some tools
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Semgrep (rules: p/default, p/security-audit, p/typescript, p/secrets)
        uses: returntocorp/semgrep-action@v1
        with:
          config: p/default
          generateSarif: true
        env: { SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SEMGREP_APP_TOKEN }} }
      - name: ESLint security rules (free, zero-config, catches the obvious)
        run: pnpm lint:security
      - name: CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with:
          languages: typescript,javascript
          queries: security-extended
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3

  # ── 2. SCA: every commit, and a hard policy on the diff.
  sca:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: OSV-Scanner (better advisory coverage than npm audit)
        run: |
          curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/osv-scanner/main/install.sh | sh
          osv-scanner scan source -r . --format json --output osv.json || true
          node scripts/osv-policy.mjs osv.json     # fail only on high/critical in *direct* deps
      - name: Licence check
        run: pnpm licenses list --json | npx license-checker --onlyAllow 'MIT;Apache-2.0;BSD-3-Clause;ISC;BSD-2-Clause' --production

  # ── 3. Secret scanning: pre-commit AND full history.
  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - name: Gitleaks (current tree + full history)
        run: |
          docker run -v "$PWD:/repo" zricethezav/gitleaks:latest detect \
            --source=/repo --report-format=sarif --report-path=gitleaks.sarif --redact
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()
        with: { sarif_file: gitleaks.sarif }

  # ── 4. Container + IaC scanning on every build.
  image-and-iac:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t $IMAGE:$SHA .
      - run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 --ignore-unfixed $IMAGE:$SHA
      - run: trivy fs --scanners misconfig,secret --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .

  # ── 5. DAST: nightly, against a staging deploy. Open-source and free.
  dast:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    needs: [deploy-staging]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Start ZAP baseline scan (passive: safe against a live app)
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/zap/wrk" -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable \
            zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.example.test \
              -c zap-baseline.conf -r zap-report.html -J zap-report.json -I || true
      - name: Start ZAP full scan (active: attacks; run against an isolated environment only)
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/zap/wrk" -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable \
            zap-full-scan.py -t https://staging.example.test -r zap-full.html || true
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: zap-report, path: zap-*.html }

// scripts/security-policy.mjs
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'

const SARIF = JSON.parse(readFileSync(process.argv[2], 'utf8'))
const findings = SARIF.runs.flatMap((r) =>
  r.results.map((res) => ({
    rule: res.ruleId,
    severity: res.level,
    file: res.locations?.[0]?.physicalLocation?.artifactLocation?.uri,
    line: res.locations?.[0]?.physicalLocation?.region?.startLine,
  })),
)

// 1. Fail on anything CRITICAL/HIGH unless it is baselined.
const baseline = new Set(JSON.parse(readFileSync('.security-baseline.json', 'utf8')).accepted)  // [{rule, file, line?}]
const NEW = findings.filter(
  (f) => ['critical', 'error', 'high'].includes(f.severity) &&
         !baseline.some((b) => b.rule === f.rule && b.file === f.file),
)

console.log(`scanned: ${findings.length} findings; new high/critical: ${NEW.length}; baselined: ${baseline.size}`)
if (process.argv.includes('--max-new') && NEW.length > Number(process.env.MAX_NEW_FINDINGS ?? 0)) {
  for (const f of NEW) console.error(`  ${f.severity} ${f.rule} ${f.file}:${f.line}`)
  process.exit(1)
}

// 2. Fail if the baseline has shrunk: a fixed finding must have its entry removed.
if (process.argv.includes('--ratchet')) {
  const stillPresent = new Set(findings.map((f) => `${f.rule}|${f.file}`))
  const stale = [...baseline].filter((b) => !stillPresent.has(`${b.rule}|${b.file}`))
  if (stale.length > 0) {
    console.error(`::error::${stale.length} baseline entries no longer match a finding. Remove them from .security-baseline.json.`)
    process.exit(1)
  }
}

topics.title: Test data management, PII, and GDPR in test suites
topics.description: Test data management, PII, and GDPR in test suites within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: Test data management
Test data is personal data if it identifies a natural person. A realistic name and email is personal data. A customer record copied from production is personal data and is almost certainly unlawful.

The lawful basis for using real personal data in testing is almost never legitimate interest if you did not ask the people, and is never "it is only in a test environment". Copying production data into a test database is a processing activity requiring a lawful basis, and it also breaches most data-processing agreements (DPAs) and security commitments.
Data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)) requires you to use synthetic data where synthetic data suffices -- which it usually does.
Storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) means test data needs a retention policy and an automated deletion job, not an assumption.

Subject access and erasure (Arts. 12, 17) apply to test data if it is personal data: a data subject who asks to be deleted has a right that reaches your test databases and your fixtures. This is a real operational problem, and the standard mitigation is that you never had their data.
Cross-border transfer: an EU subject's data in a US test environment is a Chapter V transfer requiring a lawful mechanism.
The safe-harbour answer: generate synthetic data with no relationship to any natural person, document that, and you have largely removed the problem.
Retention and expiry -- the operational side of storage limitation
A DLP gate for CI, so this never regresses
The "we needed real data" conversation, and the honest answer

Synthetic data is less realistic than the real thing, so it misses bugs that depend on the *shape* of real data (skewed distributions, long strings, mixed encodings, specific referential patterns). The mitigation is to make your generator's distributions match your production's *statistics* (not its values) -- and to document the statistics you matched.
commonMistakes: the free-text note is not a control; a control is a check that fails the build.

topics.title: The economics of testing: pyramid vs trophy, and coverage that pays
topics.description: The economics of testing: pyramid vs trophy, and coverage that pays within Quality Beyond Tests.
keyConcepts: The two shapes, side by side
Which shape to use, and the reasoning behind the choice
The economics, quantified

E2E's value per engineering hour is the lowest and its CI/triage cost is the highest. 28 tests costing 3 hours a week and 45 minutes of triage per failure. That is the argument for *fewer, better* E2E tests, not for more.

Component tests have the best ratio in a front-end project, which is precisely the trophy's argument: they catch real wiring bugs (providers, queries, routing, event handling) at a third of the E2E cost and a fiftieth of the triage cost.
The tier that is cheap and ungated is worth keeping ungated (perf, visual): running them on every PR costs more than it catches.
Triage time, not runtime, is the dominant E2E cost. 45 minutes per failure is the real number, and it is driven by the quality of your traces and failure messages, not by the test's speed.
It corresponds to a stated behaviour or risk, not to a line of code. (If you cannot name the behaviour, you are writing a change-detector.)
It fails when the behaviour breaks. Verify this by mutating the implementation (9.4.4). If it does not fail, the test is not paying.
It is deterministic and fast enough to run often. A 3-minute integration test run 40 times a week is fine; a 3-minute test run once is decoration.
Its maintenance cost is bounded. If it will need rewriting on every refactor, the tier is wrong (implementation-detail test) or the seam is wrong.
The behaviour it covers is more likely to change than to be deleted, or it is so critical that even a stable behaviour must stay verified (money, permissions, safety).

keyConcepts: The architecture decision that makes everything else possible
The five test layers for an LLM feature, cheapest first
Layer 1: Pure unit tests of the prompt-adjacent logic
Layer 2: Contract tests against a recorded model (or a local model)
Layer 4: The LLM-as-judge harness, with the anti-patterns named
The four LLM-as-judge anti-patterns, and their fixes
Layer 5: Non-determinism handling, which is a test-design question
The safety and abuse tests -- the ones with legal weight
The evaluation pipeline: what runs where

Property-based and distribution-based assertions are weaker than exact assertions. They can miss a subtle quality regression. The compensation is a *rubric-judged* eval set with per-category thresholds and a human-reviewed sample, which catches the subtle cases the properties miss. You accept a noisier, weaker signal in exchange for it not being a coin flip.

An LLM-as-judge is a second model with its own biases and variance. Validating it against a human-labelled gold set is mandatory before you trust it, and it is a real ongoing cost (a labelled set, periodic re-validation, occasional judge upgrades).

Pinning the model version slows adoption. New model versions are usually better, and you are locked out until you re-baseline. The mitigation is a scheduled weekly job that runs the full eval against the candidate version and produces a comparison report, so upgrading becomes a decision with data rather than a gamble.
